subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF NAVAL OFFICER AS TO ENEMY SUBMARINE OPERATIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF NAVAL OFFICER AS TO ENEMY SUBMARINE OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services whether the statement made by Rear-Admiral Brodeur at Quebec a few days ago was made with his consent and, if not, whether it represents the opinion of the government?
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): As to the first question, the statement attributed to Rear-Admiral Brodeur in the newspapers yesterday afternoon was not made with my knowledge or consent. I believe the second question is answered by the answer I have already given.
The statement purports to represent the opinion of that officer, although he qualifies it somewhat by saying it may be, or it is possible, that the Germans might have a certain number of submarines. However until I have a more definite record of what the rear-admiral did say, I should like to refrain from any further comment upon it.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF NAVAL OFFICER AS TO ENEMY SUBMARINE OPERATIONS
speechtext:
In view of Mr. Churchill's statement in the House of Commons that the number of sinkings should not be given out, why should an officer stationed at Washington interfere?
Libel and Slander

I would ask for a board of inquiry in connection with this matter. There should be an admiralty board; the rear-admiral should be dismissed from the service and not sent back to Washington. It is the most mischievous statement ever made and invites invasion. They never had five hundred submarines in the Atlantic at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF NAVAL OFFICER AS TO ENEMY SUBMARINE OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word on that point. The gentleman in question is a rear-admiral of the Royal Canadian Navy, and the fact that he happens to be stationed at Washington at the moment does not take away from his standing as an officer of the Royal Canadian Navy.
As to the making of statements respecting numbers I would point out that numbers of enemy ships have been conjectured from time to time by men in Great Britain, in Canada and in the United States, some of whom were and others were not in the services. I should prefer that such conjectures be not made. But, as I say, until I see what the rear-admiral really did say, from his own notes, I believe I should refrain from any further comment.

subtopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL ATTORNEYS GENERAL IN ENFORCEMENT OF FEDERAL LAW

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL ATTORNEYS GENERAL IN ENFORCEMENT OF FEDERAL LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to point out that while Hansard of Tuesday, page 657, is perfectly correct, in reporting the proceedings the Canadian Press said that I had said that "old religious controversies had been forgotten by many and they wondered why they should be continued." Those words are ascribed to me. They were not mine but were those of Reverend Mr. Toplady, writer of "Rock of Ages." The words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as reported on page 664 of Hansard, are perfectly correct. I have been told four times by predecessors of the Minister of Justice, who is also Attorney General of Canada, that an attorney general should not be asked to give a legal opinion to the house. The law quoted by the Prime Minister in connection with libel and slander is correct, except for the qualification that I make, namely that the enforcement of all federal law is for the provincial attorneys general. This is the first time during the many years I have been in the house that I have known an attorney general to give a legal opinion, especially on religion. I do not ask the minister to reply to-day; he can look up the page of Hansard of last year when on his estimates, we were discussing the newspaper bill I had introduced also in 1936, 1937 and 1938. At that time I asked the former minister, Mr. Lapointe, if an attorney general could give a legal opinion, and he said I was correct; that the rule was he should not. He asked me if I knew the reason and I said that I did. The reason is that should an attorney general appear in court as a litigant it might be said, as was said in England, that he should not give a legal opinion because when he appears before a judge, the judge might consider that the case was being prejudged and there might be a mistrial. I ask the attorney general to look up what his predecessors said. No legal opinion should be given to the house by the present minister and I ask him to look up the statement.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): I am sorry, but I have not understood what the hon. member said.

The Address-Mr. Lockhart

subtopic: JURISDICTION OF PROVINCIAL ATTORNEYS GENERAL IN ENFORCEMENT OF FEDERAL LAW
speechtext: I ask the minister for a reply. The only trouble is that it is sometimes convenient, as it was last Tuesday, to give a legal opinion for propaganda purposes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. E. Harris (Grey-Bruce) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Graydon.
Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln) : Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I gave notice that there were some observations I desired to make arising out of certain events of more recent days. I desire to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Dienfen-baker), particularly his criticism of the explanatory letter which has been sent out by the director of selective service and attested to by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). I feel definitely that equality of service has not been achieved and I think the crux of the whole situation is that we lack a coordinated war effort in this country.
As I say, events of the last few days necessitate my making a few comments in this house. I want to remind hon. members again of the statement made about a year ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which indicated definitely that all farm labour would be frozen, I think it was as of March 23, 1942. I should like to outline as briefly as I can what has happened since that time. The regional office of the national selective service referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) is located in my district, and I commend him for the remarks he has made in this connection because I know something about this particular office.
The Prime Minister's statement with respect to farm help was expected to provide some relief for the general situation. But that was a year ago. Farmers' sons are still being called. I received three letters to-day asking me for an explanation of what the Prime Minister's words meant, the statement that he made a year ago. Our farmers have been asked by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to increase their production programme. Is it any wonder therefore that they are upset about the labour situation which affects the increased production of foodstuffs for which the minister has asked? The urgency has become so great that I am prompted to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) a question, and I shall include also the Minister of Labour. If these men are as important as was indicated twelve months ago by the Prime Minister, and as is indicated now by the Minister of Labour, can the Minister of National Defence state that they are not being accepted at the present time when they go to enlist? When this type of man presents himself for enlistment, is he told to go back where he belongs? I know that he is not.
I have visited some of these lavishly constructed recruiting offices-incidentally I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) had better check on the cost of some of these recruiting centres-and I find that they grab any young man they can possibly get their hands on. The recruiting office in Ottawa has been closed up for some time, but in the last day or two the trumpets have been blaring forth again. I ask the Minister of National Defence to check up on that so that the people of this country will know that the urgent need for food is actually being recognized.
Before the Minister of Finance launches his next budget of five billion dollars, which is the amount mentioned in the press I should like to bring to his attention the fact that it is generally felt by the people of this country that there is wasteful expenditure going on under many government departments. Somebody said not very long ago that we *have strange men at Ottawa. Perhaps some will say that includes some in this chamber, but it is not to them I refer. According to the press of February 20 last a gentleman who until recently held a high place at Ottawa in the timber control administration, and is reputed to be one of the greatest authorities on timber and lumber in Canada, addressing the Ontario Retail Lumber Dealers association in the Royal York hotel, Toronto, i® reported to have used these words:
Don't depend upon Ottawa to lead the course in Canada's lumber programme; those in the industry itself must map out the timber policy and vigorously present this to the federal authorities.
Mr. A. S. Nicholson then went on to make reference to his sudden resignation. The report continues:
Prior to Mr. Nicholson's address, a resolution was unanimously passed expressing the continued opposition of the lumbermen toward the efforts that have been made, and are being made, by Wartime Housing Limited to encroach upon the field of permanent dwelling houses. It was claimed that Wartime Housing Limited was building great numbers of permanent dwellings valued at from $4,000 to $6,000 and that "this monopoly" was bankrupting legitimate builders.
He warned the retail lumber men of certain dangers in the second-hand lumber situation,
The Address-Mr. Lockhart

and I shall refer to this a little later. There is one other paragraph in the press report which I should like to quote:
One very high official told me I tried to run the timber board too economically and that I worked too hard.
I wish anyone who has lived in Ottawa for a part of each year during the past few years would tell this house where economy is being practised in any government department in this city.
For a year and more everybody who is engaged in the production or distribution of foodstuffs in this country has been trying to convince the government that the man-power situation is in a muddle, that things are in a state of chaos which must inevitably lead to a situation that will become absolutely beyond control. Members in every part of this house have reechoed these sentiments. One hon. member suggested taking men out of the army temporarily and putting them where there was essential work to do. I think every hon. member has had brought to his attention the plight of farmers who have been deprived of help which was vitally needed, and I think everyone realizes how difficult it is to get a man released from the army once he falls into the clutches of the military authorities. But the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has asked for increased production of foodstuffs. Last year the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. MacDiarmid) made an urgent appeal to the government that help be provided for the farmers. By a strange coincidence I was informed only yesterday of three or four farms in his county, large tracts of the best land in that splendid agricultural district where the farmer has been left with no help at all. These are farms which formerly carried from twenty-five to forty or fifty head of cattle and other stock in proportion, yet to-day only the farmer and his wife are left to carry on the work, and the consequence is that the stock must be reduced and implements are lying idle. I can understand, therefore, the urgency of the appeal made a year ago by the hon. member for Glengarry, but I cannot understand why it fell on deaf ears, particularly since he is on the government side of the house. In my own county the same conditions prevail in many districts; good buildings and splendid machinery are not being utilized. Some way must be found in which the minister and the Department of Agriculture can put their increased food production programme into effect.
Somebody may say: It is easy enough to criticize but how is the situation to be corrected? That is a fair question. In reply I

should like to put on Hansard the opinion of a body of men who understand present-day conditions. The Minister of Agriculture may already have seen this resolution, but if not I shall be glad to furnish him with a copy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He can read it in Hansard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would thank the hon. gentleman not to interrupt, because I intend to read this whether he likes it or not. Before doing so, may I pause to remind the house of the number of members of the cabinet who have been to Britain during the past year or two. I am not criticizing them for going, and if I am wrong in any comments I make I ask that I be corrected.
First let me say that I am informed on good authority that many hundreds of thousands of acres-in fact, I was told by one source that it was nearly three million acres-of good tillable soil in Great Britain has been taken over for defence purposes. We will put the amount at three millions in round figures. I am also informed on good authority from over there that an equivalent amount of land, or more, is now under cultivation in Britain in excess of what was under cultivation when the war broke out. It is not important for my purposes whether the figure is three millions or three and a half millions; certainly great areas of land have been put under cultivation. This result, I am told, has been accomplished through the appointing of committees of responsible men in every county or borough, vested with powers to deal with this situation. Over there they do not want irresponsible controllers who are not accountable to parliament. Their committees in the several counties and boroughs have authority to this extent, that if a particular farmer-say, for example, my friend the hon. member for Glengarry-is in need of help, the local board can go to industry-yes, and to the armed forces-and obtain the men necessary to keep production at the peak in that particular area. If the statements I have made are correct, I wonder why the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour have not developed a similar system here in view of the fact that the production of so many farms in this country has been seriously depleted.
I have here a resolution presented by my own county council, to which I will ask hon. members to listen, and to which I shall briefly refer. Though I have had no contact with my county council, I know the resolution was presented by two ex-wardens whom I know to be outstanding men. As for their polities, so far as I know they are of opposite political views. However, that makes no difference;

The Address-Mr. Lockhart
they are excellent farmers. Here is the resolution-I will send a copy to the Minister of Agriculture:
Whereas the shortage of man-power is the biggest obstacle in the way of Canadian farmers reaching this years' food production goals, and
Whereas there is no source from which this labour may be secured except by securing the assistance of urban people and by cooperating with each other,
Therefore be it resolved:
1.	That the council of the county of Lincoln recommend to the federal government that a qualified man be appointed for approximately each 20,000 of rural population, which in the county of Lincoln would mean the appointment of two qualified men.
2.	That the clerical work be done in the offices of the provincial agricultural representatives.
May I pause at this point to tell the Minister of Agriculture that I have it on good authority, regarding the operation of the agricultural offices in Great Britain, that there is no increase, or practically none, in staff, and that the work is done out in the field by competent men who have authority to act in this connection.
3.	That the duties of the men so appointed shall be to see that the various phases of agriculture are organized and that these organizations cooperate one with the other for the achievement of the one aim which is the production of more food.
4.	That to aid in the attainment of this goal of production of more food the following suggestions be recommended for consideration of the federal government.
(a)	That city and all urban residents be encouraged to devote some time to farm work by supplying them with extra gasoline to provide transportation to and from the farm, and that the men appointed to carry out the field work, of this war production programme, be given the power, to issue these coupons, when he investigates, and finds that these urban and city people are working on the farm, and driving their own car back and forth to the farm.
(b)	That small groups of farmers cooperate to save much food.
(c)	That sows, gilts, cows and heifers be kept in production instead of being butchered.
(d)	That an increase be encouraged on some farms of extra sows, cows, extra acres of grain, potatoes, tomatoes and other fruits and vegetables and also soy beans.
(e)	That the planting of victory gardens be encouraged and stimulated on farms.
(f)	That we are quite agreed with the present government policy of price control but would suggest that a floor be put under the price of all agricultural products in order to ensure the maintenance of the present production of foodstuffs and further encourage others to do their utmost.
Having received yesterday the resolution which I have read, and having gleaned a good deal of information from the old land as to how these matters are being handled there, I
am moved to ask why some of these most effective methods, of which ministers surely must have knowledge, are not put into effect in Canada.
I want to say a word about egg production, since there is quite a number of small producers in my area. The Minister of Agriculture tells us he wants more eggs. You cannot have eggs unless you have baby chicks. I do not know why this subject was ever referred to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson), whom I see in his seat. I understand that he heard much about baby chicks when he was in the city of Hamilton-as did the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross). Apparently this industry, not only in Hamilton but in other places of which I have heard, is completely robbed of the experienced help which is necessary properly to produce these chicks. Perhaps the Minister of Labour would be good enough to get out another letter and explain the situation; it would be very helpful under the present circumstances.
Small producers in my riding tell me that they have difficulty in getting as much as twenty-eight cents for their present production of eggs, and that distribution facilities are such that it is almost impossible to find any medium whereby they can dispose of their production. In a letter I have here they urge me to find out whether there is any medium by which they can get rid of their surplus eggs, and they ask definitely that a bottom price be put on eggs so that they can get at least the cost of production and a little something to pay them for their labours. I would remind the Minister of Labour that if we do not have chicks we will not have eggs and we will not have hens, and the minister will not get his quota of eggs unless he does something to encourage these people by providing them with experienced help. This applies also to pork and beef, and I could deal further with the situation as it affects many other commodities. It all comes back to the muddled man-power policy we have had for the past three or more years.
I want to say a word to the Minister of Finance in regard to his budget of five billion dollars, which must be raised by taxation and other means during the coming year. I am going to voice the sentiments of a great many people in my own community who are asking one question. The Prime Minister has said that we need a reallocation of manpower and woman-power. The Minister of Labour has attempted to carry out this reallocation by regulation, which regulation has been further explained and clarified. This being so, why is it necessary to keep on adding factory extensions all over the coun-
The Address-Mr. Lockhart

try? This is being done in my own district, and I suppose in other districts as well. I know of one large addition in my own city which has been begun just recently. Then we have contracts for hostels and other buildings. I do urge upon the Minister of Finance that he bring pressure to bear upon the proper authorities to let us have in this house a real picture of the money that is being spent on hostels, staff houses and so on, many of which are not half filled. I have personal knowledge as to that. People are beginning to wonder why this reckless expenditure should continue. I urge upon the minister that he see to it that proper and adequate information is given this house so that when the people are asked to raise five billion dollars next year they may know the money will be properly spent. I am told that a hostel to take care of five hundred persons costs more than a quarter of a million dollars. That is a lot of hard-earned money which must be raised by a good many people, and it is about time we knew how this money is to be spent.
I should like now to refer to the construction of permanent housing units by Wartime Housing Limited, to which reference was made by Mr. Nicholson in his address in Toronto. Is it any wonder that the building contractors and all the various trades associated with the construction of houses, one of the greatest industries in this country, are organizing to protest against the way this is being carried on? I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is not careful he may have another political group with which to contend. These men are sincere; they have made representations to the government, and I can tell the Prime Minister now that he will not have heard the last from them if he continues to allow Wartime Housing Limited to interfere further with private enterprise in the construction of permanent houses.
While I am on the question of the construction of houses, let me say that before we are asked to vote a five billion dollar budget we should be supplied with full information as to the amount of money that has been spent on war-time housing up to the present. I ask particularly that the expenditures in the city of Hull be laid before this house. A year or so ago we were told that the cost then had reached $3,800 per unit. I have been over there; I have looked into the situation, and I know a little about the construction of houses. We have seven or eight hundred of these war-time houses in my own city, and it is high time we knew where the money is going that is being spent

in the housing programme in Hull. That goes also for war-time housing all over the country. I am not questioning the need for a certain amount of this type of construction. No doubt the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) had a problem on his hands, but surely it is time we knew what money has been spent on this kind of thing and what has been the cost per unit, not only in Hull but all over the dominion. It might be interesting if someone would page the mayor of Hamilton in connection with this "permanent" construction, because I know he has some very strong ideas in connection with it. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue will see him in that regard, because we were told that a programme was to be developed in Hamilton, though I believe there has been a delay of some kind. I am asking, however, that the fullest possible information be given this house in connection with Wartime Housing Limited, if not before the budget comes down at least a reasonable time before the people have to raise this huge amount of money.
I want to say a word about fuel. Back in the middle of December, 1942, I believe it was the Minister of Finance who told us we were short eight million tons of fuel. What has been done during the present heating season to relieve that situation? Hon. members on the opposite side have told us no provision was made for labour to bring wood out to the highways in order that it might be brought to the people. I remember reading a news item not very long ago stating that the town of Lindsay, in the Haliburton area, had no fuel. Surely if a coordinated plan of any kind is being developed for this season there should be no shortage of wood for fuel in the town of Lindsay or the Haliburton district. What is being done? It would be very helpful to hon. members and to the thousands of people living in *war-time houses in areas where they cannot get wood, because of transportation difficulties, if they were told they need have no fear of not being able to heat their homes next winter; for I know many are suffering this year. This house and these people should be told whether there is a definite programme to relieve the situation. It must be remembered that these war-time houses have only a little fuel box at the back door holding only half a ton of coal. They must depend upon the distributors of fuel to supply them every ten days or two weeks, and the labour situation is such that I know of one firm which is printing signs saying that it has plenty of fuel but that people must get it in their own wheelbarrows. Thus the man-power situation affects our whole economy. Some controller

The Address-Division
not long ago conceived the bright idea of spreading the news that there was bituminous coal in abundance in certain areas, and urging people to burn it. Surely the Minister of Munitions and Supply, knowing the equipment used by these people, must know that they cannot burn that soft, mine-run bituminous coal. A few days afterwards someone got a brain wave-to tell this to the people; and in their desperation they used it. I think it was in a Toronto paper we read that three or four people had died from coal gas poisoning. Within a week after this flood of literature about burning soft coal went over the country these people, who are munition workers-they cannot get a house unless they are-were putting soft coal into small firepots twelve inches in diameter. The result was that away went the lid and the door, and they woke up in the morning to find the place full of coal gas.
The supply of anthracite coal must be distributed where it is needed. Into the northern areas, where there is wood in abundance, no anthracite should go. What we need is a man-power policy to see that wood is got out in proper time so that there shall be no fear of lack of fuel for the winter of 1943-44..
Our man-power muddle is terrible. Here is one thing I wish to call to the attention of the Minister of National Defence. Yesterday morning a young man, a skilled toolmaker and machinist who has been working in an industry in this city for three and a half years, said to me, "I am disgusted." I am not going to tell the whole story, but he told me about production in the plant. He said, "I am going to see if I can enlist." I wonder if it is possible for a young man deliberately to leave an industry after three and a half years' special training, in order to enlist.
It is high time someone told us where we have to go and what we have to do. I have felt this for some time. I ask the government to give us some lead in this respect. From the press all across the country as well as in this House of Commons comes the call for a balanced man-power plan. Surely the Prime Minister and his advisers must be alive to the situation; surely they see that the man-and woman-power of this country must be reallocated at once. In my opinion there is only one solution and it is the enactment of national compulsory selective service legislation covering every part of this country and for every war service. This is the only thing I can see that will give us an all-out total war effort in Canada. Our first job is to win the war.

Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I have explained my position on the address and I shall not be long in making the remarks I wish to make now. I am always brief in addressing the Chair and I shall follow that tradition to-day.
I have been a member of this house since 1924. In the period from 1924 to 1930 I fought for the party. In the period from 1930 to 1935 I fought for my electors and also for the party which understood the work I was doing. Since 1935 I have been fighting for my constituents and also for the party which does not understand that I am working for them. In 1931 I tried to get some information about butter, because butter had been one of the controversial subjects raised by the Conservative party during the election. I got some data about butter and other dairy products. We also had a fight over the Riviere du Loup station and unemployment. In 1932 it was mostly railways, the Post Office Department and unemployment relief. In 1932-33 it was the Ottawa trade agreements. Long speeches were made on those, and we also took up statistics, radio, the Post Office Department, the redistribution bill and unemployment relief.
On page 1949 of Hansard of February 9, 1933, are to be found fifty questions which I put to the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and which have never been answered. It took a long time to draft them, but I undertook that work in order to give an opportunity to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group to give us some explanation of their policy. The former member for Humboldt was a dear friend of mine and he wrote me last year to ask for a copy of these questions.
In 1934 there was Mr. Sauve's trip to Egypt to attend the Cairo postal congress, the fight on the bureau of translation bill, trade statistics, unemployment and farm relief, and redistribution. At that time the member for Temiscouata prepared a book which was furnished to the house but the Clerk of the House informs me that it has never been used by hon. members. However, it is still kept in the vaults of parliament. This book contains the story of redistribution in the province of Quebec from 1853 to 1933 and it shows how each county was affected by each redistribution. It is there if anyone wants to refer to it. It shows what has happened to the geography of each constituency in the province of Quebec over a long period of time. If it has not been used by any hon. member of parliament since it was tabled, it may be because the redistribution bill has not come

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
before us. However, it was used by the former minister of justice and the former minister of public works when they discussed this matter with two members of the Bennett government, Mr. Duranleau and Sir George Perley.
The point I want to make is that I was not a member of the committee. The one who represented the province of Quebec was a gentleman who made a speech about the Ottawa agreements in which he quoted four pages of a speech which had been made by Mr. Bennett, then prime minister, and four pages of a speech which had been delivered by the chief of the Liberal party-eight pages, really, four on each side-and that was the member's speech. It was so bad that it was struck off the record. He was the one who represented the province of Quebec on the committee, and since he did not do his work, I had to do it. The Liberal federation was paid to do this work. The representative of the province of Quebec on the committee did nothing. I had to do his work myself. Once when I was working on it, a member of the federation came to my office and spoke to me. I said to him, "Give me a chance to do your work. Don't disturb me when I am doing your work." I was doing it to help the members and to prevent the Bennett government from destroying the former constituency.
In 1935 what was discussed mostly was unemployment, external trade, and taxation. At the close of the session I was asked to prepare a tabulation of all taxation which had been imposed by Bennett each year. Not a single one of those taxes was removed1 by the party, although that tabulation was used as propaganda in the election of 1935, being issued as a leaflet. We complained of the sugar tax, but it was left where it was. I made a tabulation of all the taxes, and it served hon. members during that election. We also spoke during that session of tax-free bonds.
Besides that, another thing was done-the preparation of a report on unemployment. That report was carefully made and was well received by the press. A minister, who was not then a member of the house, wrote me a letter dated June 19, 1935, in which he said :
It is the most able analysis of the situation I have seen and will be exceedingly useful to me.
This was done to show that Mr. Bennett's unemployment policy was no good, and that the unemployment problem deserved careful consideration. I was successful in distributing copies to every member of the House of
Commons in 1935. In the following year Hon. Mr. Rogers, who was then minister of labour, had a second edition made of that report and sent to each member of parliament, especially to the new members who had not had an opportunity of securing it before. I was often told by the late Mr. Gordon, when he was minister of labour in the Bennett cabinet, that it was impossible to secure data on the unemployed in Canada. About that time a congress of municipalities was meeting at the Chateau Laurier, and I asked the mayors who were in convention there if they could not supply me with some information on the unemployed. Their first answer was no, but finally I got some information from them. It took a long time. I did that at no cost to the country except for paper and printing, which does not amount to much. I sent telegrams out at my own expense. I made a report which gave a true picture of unemployment, and it showed that Mr. Bennett was not true in the words he put into the mouth of his excellency in each of the speeches from the throne at the opening and closing of the sessions. I had the great honour of hearing Hon. Mr. Rogers, minister of labour at that time, state in the house that that report was the basis of the unemployment policy of the government.
Then I asked for a complete report on the unemployed in my constituency. It was prepared by two very able men:	Mr. Lafortune, a former controller of the city of Ottawa council and a very well-known man, and Mr. Begin, who was one of the appointees of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). These men lived in my county for several months and took the trouble to go into 1.200 homes of unemployed settlers, many of whom had no cattle and no horses, some of whom had six animals (six chickens), another only one animal and it was a dog; while some had an ox or a horse. Some had a cow which was used in place of a horse or ox and also used to provide milk for the children, but the milk was not very good coming from a cow that was used as a beast of burden.
After the session of 1935 the Ottawa Journal wrote an editorial about the member for Temiscouata, from which I read this last paragraph:
So, let's not be too shocked over Mr. Pouliot, Hypocrites that we are, must of us will probably say out loud that the man is an impossible partisan but that will only be because we like to have other people say of us that we're fair and reasonable. Secretly, we have to admit that Jean-Francois has merely had the courage-or
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

perhaps folly-to speak out what most of us think; that he's expressed what most of us are slaves to.
And the thing isn't as bad as it seems. The story of our whole party system, which hasn't worked too badly, tells us that.
Mr. Lafortune and Mr. Begin made their report. It was a thick and very comprehensive report, well got up and showing everything. After the report was made, an agreement was signed by the dominion government with the provincial governments that it would not pay any unemployment relief. Therefore the report was of no use. But I gave it to one of my provincial colleagues, who got in touch with Mr. Godbout and it was one of the reasons why the provincial government of Quebec has been doing much along this line.
In the session of 1936 there was the loan by Mr. Bennett, without consulting his colleagues, of $60,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Then I had some little difficulty with the Speaker. Although he forgot what was the procedure and practice of the house by asking me to withdraw certain things I had said, although they were innocent words I had used I withdrew them just to show my good will and to save him trouble.
Then there was unemployment and social insurance, which I fought and bitterly complained about. Then there was a piece of legislation to repeal the economic council.
You know, sir, I believe that, when a policy is enunciated by the party, it binds us for a very long time until it is proved that the party has been wrong in submitting it. There was a fight in 1930 about the British tariff. In my humble view the policy of the government was good. At the time the only decrease in our trade was in shipments of grain. The purpose of the new trade agreements was to give a kind of premium or prize to our British customers, and therefore I supported the agreements. When the party came back into power in 1936, as we had been fighting the Ottawa agreements, with the exception of two for which our leaders voted, I thought it proper to ask for the repeal of chapter 2, of 23-24 George V, 1933, and to substitute therefor chapter 13 of 20-21, George V, 1930, the effect of which would have been to replace the Bennett trade agreements with our own. I was very much surprised when the Minister of Finance of the day, Mr. Dunning, rose to a point of order; he contended that my motion was not in order. That was on March 10, 1936. On April 6 following I asked for the ruling of His Honour, the Speaker, but no ruling had been given at the end of the session, not even when we heard the boom of the gun that announced the prorogation speech.

In 1937 it was the Canadian National Railways, unemployment, and national defence. At the time, I voted against some estimates of the Department of National Defence because I wanted some order in the department, and I wanted the bureaucracy which was supreme in the department to be curbed. One reason I took this action was that I was invited to a private reception given by a top "brass hat". By the way, when that "brass hat" was in a theatre of war he was weeping all the time; that was the way he served his country during that war. I do not know whether the glasses were full of tears or of liquor, but the liquor was very good. There was a distribution of champagne at that reception. Oh, it was fine and there was plenty of it. But I wondered whether there was something wrong there at the time.
In 1938 we fought the divorce courts and divorce bills. In that session there was also a civil service committee, to which I referred yesterday, and an unemployment relief bill. At that time I sent to the Liberal party a memorandum on the situation in tne province of Quebec, with particular reference to the padlock law.
In 1939 there was the question of the library of parliament. We fought the central mortgage bank bill, and the bill was dropped; those who were to act under the bill were appointed but they were not given the power to act. The thing was stopped. Therefore we were right on that. We opposed the national defence board, the transfer of the purchasing branch of the Department of National Defence to the Minister of National Defence; and on that also we were right. It was a service to the party, in order that the party should have less trouble. Also we complained about the deputy minister of finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, because what they were doing was being done behind the back of the House of Commons, with the assistance of the intelligentsia of this country.
At the special session of 1930, when the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett rose in his full glory to state that such unemployment as existed would be cured by high tariffs, the member for Temiscouta, who was sitting on a back bench, was the only one who rose to call for a division. The fact is not reported in the papers of the house but it was recorded by the parliamentary correspondent of Le Devoir, in Montreal.
These are a few things which I wanted to tell the house.
Since the war began I have done my best to do two things-to help the soldiers, and

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
to have a fair application of the man-power regulations. How far we have succeeded wrill no doubt be known in due course. It is very difficult at times to do what we want to do for the soldiers and for the civilian population. The work here is hard. There are only twenty-four hours to a day and every available minute is occupied. Sometimes we are sorry the days are not longer, because we have so much to do.
There are other things we have done-things which have been done in the interests of the party. My contention is that our actions should be in agreement with what is being said in public. Sometimes we are exposed to disagreement and to controversy with this or that hon. member. For instance, I had a controversy with the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Bruce), because he had insinuated that the Prime Minister was not well qualified to be the head of the government in war time. I was, I admit, unpleasant to the hon. member for Parkdale. I have nothing against him; he is an eminent member of the medical profession and a prominent citizen of Ontario; but I had to fight him on this issue in order to defend the head of the Liberal party.
More than that, on February 21, 1941, I used strong language with regard to some ministers, but it was because of certain intrigues which were then going on. What I have never said is that, in the forenoon preceding that speech, I telephoned to most of the English-speaking ministers outside the province of Quebec to tell them that there was an intrigue being made for the formation of a union government and that if it was successful they would be thrown overboard. One of the ministers, whom naturally I will not mention, told me that those who were against him were also those who were against me. What touched me very deeply-for I had not expected it, and had not telephoned to the Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe about it, although I had spoken here on the Friday afternoon- was that, while I was at home the following Monday, I heard over the radio that Mr. Lapointe had spoken in the house on exactly the same lines on that Monday, which showed that we saw eye to eye on this matter and that we both were defending the Prime Minister against all intrigues directed against him.
You know, sir, the story of the St. Bernard dog which barked very loudly and tugged at his master's clothes to get him out into the storm. He was kicked, but he was insistent. He was so persistent that finally the master put on his winter clothes, went out, and found one of his men who had been hurt in a fall on the rocks during the storm. So that sometimes, though we do things which are
very unpleasant, they are for a good purpose. It is always easier to listen to those who are close to us, but there are some who, though close to us for a time, leave us afterwards.
I have in mind the case of Mr. Victor Sifton. I remember that one day during the summer, about the end of July, I was going down the plaza here. I saw a long car approaching, and someone put his head out of the window and shouted, "Victor! Victor!" It was the Minister of National Defence who wanted to see Mr. Sifton again before he went back to Winnipeg. There was no harm in that; but since he has been in Winnipeg, Mr. Sifton, who knows more about the Department of National Defence than any other civilian, has complained bitterly about the bad influence of the brass hats.
There is something else which I regret very much; it is based upon information appearing in the press, which I presume is correct. When the bombing crew who dropped bombs on Germany one morning and came to Canada the same day were here in Ottawa, they were photographed with various members of the cabinet. For some reason or other the Minister of National Defence was not at hand, and the Prime Minister said, "Where is Ralston? I want him to be photographed with me." I suppose that is natural, because the Prime Minister relies upon the Minister of National Defence and wants to share his glory with him; but the gentleman who told me about the incident was surprised that the Prime Minister should be so insistent upon having his picture taken with the Minister of National Defence. These are minor things, but centuries ago Plutarch said that it is by small things we judge great men. I do not desire to play the role of Cassandra; speaking about ambitions,
I have none. However, it is perfectly legitimate for the leader of any party to expect to be able to rely upon his close supporters.
At the time of the vote on the plebiscite I was in Montreal, where I met a prominent citizen of Quebec, who asked how things were going here in Ottawa. I told him how they were going, and he said, "The Prime Minister will go, and he will be replaced by so and so," . naming one of his colleagues. A little later I was here in Ottawa, and in one of the corridors of the building I saw another colleague of the Prime Minister who looked like a conspirator. Sometimes it is interesting to watch what is going on. Let me tell the Prime Minister that he can rely upon his humblest friends, even though at times they may differ with him on certain points. It is most difficult to terminate associations we have had for a very long time with colleagues with whom we have been working with a common aim.
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

We have come to know each other; we have tried to help each other, and we have managed to get along pretty well.
There is one further thing I desire to say. I have never said anything against any member of parliament, and I have appreciated the kindness and courtesy of the members of this house. I have been here a long time. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) is the dean of the house in point of years; the Prime Minister is next in line, and I am one of the older members. I appreciate very much the relations I have enjoyed not only with members on this side of the house but with those on the other side as well. But may I say that in my opinion it is wrong for the government to take the opposite view on every suggestion made by a member of parliament. It is always surprising to us when we are told "it is impossible" before we have an opportunity to say what we want done. Sometimes it would be a good thing for them to listen.
I could say many other things; I will say only one. It is that in my humble view the position of Minister of National Defence is a full-time job; I presume you will agree with me on that. He is even supposed to have a parliamentary secretary within a short time. Therefore I cannot conceive how at the same time the Minister of National Defence can be the perpetual acting Minister of Finance, as the Minister of Finance himself stated last year.
Nine years ago, sir, at Windsor, Ontario, the member for Temiscouata delivered a lecture on the anniversary of the death of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. At that time I quoted a few words that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had uttered in concluding a speech before a group of young men at London, Ontario, as follows:
Banish doubt and hate from your life.. Let your souls be ever open to the promptings of faith and the gentle influence of brotherly love. Be adamant against the haughty; be gentle and kind to the weak. Let your aim and purpose, in good report or ill, in victory or defeat, be so to live, so to strive, so to serve as to do your part to ever raise higher the standard of life and living.
In those few words there is a programme for every man in public life. It should not be the programme of the Liberal party only; it should be also the programme of all those who have a desire to see the greatest possible number of their fellow citizens happy and contented, living like brothers. I need not mention the numerous campaigns that have been carried on during general elections and by-elections, the articles that have been written, the editorials that have been published in Liberal newspapers or other articles that have been

mimeographed and sent to the members for distribution during several electoral campaigns. But I have always tried to see all citizens who think alike grouped together for the welfare of this country. I have supported the Prime Minister for a long time; I hope I shall be in a position to do so in the future. I do not know what the future will bring. Everything will depend upon the legislation that will come before us. But now, sir, my concluding word will be this, that this time I shall show good will by abstaining from voting on the address.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE DEPUTY SPEAKER
subsubtopic: ELECTION OF MR. JOSEPH ARTHUR BRADETTE, MEMBER FOR COCHRANE
speechtext:
The house will have observed that during the period of the long adjournment of the last session the then Deputy Speaker of the house, the Hon. Thomas Vien, was appointed to the senate, and that Colonel Yien has since been appointed Speaker of that chamber. Colonel Vien's resignation has created a vacancy in the position of Deputy Speaker of this house. I should like to read to the house the rule which governs in respect of the appointment of Deputy Speaker or Chairman of Committees when the house meets at its first session of a new parliament or when a vacancy subsequently occurs. Standing order 56 reads:
(1)	A Chairman of Committees of the house, who shall also be Deputy Speaker of the house shall be elected ... as soon as an address has been agreed on in answer to His Excellency's speech; and the member so elected shall, if in his place in the house, take the chair of all committees of the whole, including the committees of supply and ways and means, in accordance with the rules and usages which regulate the duties of a similar officer, generally designated the chairman of the committees of ways and means, in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
(2)	The member elected to serve as Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees shall be required to possess the full and practical knowledge of the language which is not that of the Speaker for the time being.
(3)	The member so elected Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees shall continue to act in that capacity until the end of the parliament for which he is elected, and in the ease of a vacancy by death, resignation or otherwise, the house shall proceed forthwith to elect a successor.
Hon. members will see from the reading of the order that the office of Chairman of Committees and Deputy Speaker of the house is a very high and honourable office, and requires, in the one to fill it, a member possessing many attainments and qualities, attainments and qualities very similar to those expected of His Honour the Speaker. The hon. member chosen for the position, inasmuch as he has to preside over the committees of the whole house and at times fill the chair of the Speaker, has to be a member who is
familiar with the procedure of the house, possessed of a full knowledge of the rules, of judicial temperment, conciliatory and yet firm, one who has qualities of discernment, judgment and quick decision, also one who, because of his courtesy and fairness, is, as nearly as it is possible to find such a one, generally acceptable to hon. members of the house as a whole. He is required in addition to possess a knowledge of the language other than that which His Honour the Speaker himself possesses. His Honour the Speaker being English-

speechtext:
-Scotch, which is even better, it is necessary that the choice should fall upon one who is possessed of a knowledge of the French language.
I am happy to say that on our side of the house we have had little difficulty in discovering a gentleman who I believe all members of the house will be prepared to agree is not only a master of the French language but has mastered the English language as well-with a shade of a Scotch accent.
I would affirm, Mr. Speaker, that we have in the person of Mr. Joseph Arthur Bradette, member of parliament for Cochrane, a gentleman who, from the reception just given the mention of his name, certainly is most acceptable to members on both sides of the house. Mr. Bradette has been a member of this House of Commons for seventeen years-or rather is now in his seventeenth year as a member-having been elected to parliament in 1926, and returned at each subsequent general election. I doubt if any other member of parliament in that period of time has been more faithful in his attendance on the proceedings of the house. During the time he has been a member he has frequently been called upon to preside over the committees of the house and has also at different times filled the chair of His Honour the Speaker. We know that at all times he performed these duties in a most creditable manner, a manner which has met with general acceptance on the part of all members of the house.
The hon. member was born in Quebec, and lived in that province for some time. Subsequently he moved to northern Ontario, where he has since resided. He has been an example to all of us in that during his period of residence in Ontario he has so completely mastered the English language that to-day he is able to speak in both French and English with a degree of fluency which few other hon. members in the house possess.
The Deputy Speaker

I have to add only that at an earlier stage of our discussions an hon. member belonging to the party sitting immediately opposite stated that when the government was called upon to make a choice of Deputy Speaker he hoped we might select the hon. member for Cochrane. I was pleased to learn in advance that the choice of the hon. member who had already been decided upon for the position of Deputy Speaker would be so acceptable to the opposition. I believe the choice will be as acceptable to the other groups in the house as it is to all hon. members on this side.
It is therefore with great pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I move, seconded by my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar):
That Joseph Arthur Bradette, Esquire, member for the electoral district of Cochrane, be appointed chairman of committees of the whole house.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE DEPUTY SPEAKER
subsubtopic: ELECTION OF MR. JOSEPH ARTHUR BRADETTE, MEMBER FOR COCHRANE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have listened with more than the usual degree of interest to the selection just announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the important position of Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees of the Whole.
One point which strikes me at once, in connection with the recipient of this very important honour, is that he is one of our Canadian citizens who has come up the hard way of life. It is my belief that if we are going to pay tribute to men in public life we ought not to lose sight of the fact that a great many of our citizens have perhaps commenced their lives under circumstances such as those which surrounded the present recipient of this honour, and we should pay special tribute to those men who have come up the hard way, like the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), and have made a success of their lives.
I believe those of us who did not have the advantage of being bom with silver spoons in our mouths appreciate more keenly the honour now conferred upon a member who has made his way up by dint of hard work, by industry, by integrity, by honesty, and by a close application to the objectives he had in mind. Not only has the hon. member for Cochrane had a number of occupations but, in addition to that, within the last few years I believe he has been called to the bar in Ontario. That perhaps, in the estimation of many hon. members, is the only thing that could be said against him.
There was a time before I entered the house when the leader who sat opposite my present seat was unmarried. At the same time there was a leader of the opposition who found
[Mr. Mackenzie Kin?. |
himself in much the same plight, and also a leader of one of the third parties who was in that unfortunate position. At the beginning of this session the Prime Minister was good enough to make some reference to the growth of certain customs and practices which he hoped would not continue. I am hopeful that his choice of this bachelor member from Cochrane will not prove to be the beginning of the growth of a custom of which the Prime Minister himself is a devoted follower.
In paying this tribute this afternoon may I congratulate the Prime Minister upon having accepted, when making this appointment, the suggestion of a member in His Majesty's Loyal Opposition. I believe it is the first time since the beginning of the session that he has not made a decision based entirely upon something brought up at the Winnipeg convention. Whether from His Honour the Speaker or from the Deputy Speaker, hon. members in His Majesty's Loyal Opposition ask only for justice, fairness and a square deal. If in a public way in his new post the hon. member for Cochrane carries on in the same way as he has while a private member in the chamber, we have reason to believe that we shall have nothing to fear from this appointment.
I congratulate the hon. member, and also the Prime Minister upon having accepted our selection upon this occasion. I hope this will not be the last occasion upon which he may be prompted to follow that procedure.

I congratulate the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), and would add that we, too, are pleased with the appointment made this afternoon. .Those of us who have been associated in various ways with the hon. member for Cochrane have grown to like him and to admire his many qualities. I am sure we shall have in our Chairman of Committees one who will follow your own example, if I may say so, and be fair at all times to all members of the house, wherever they may sit. I say to the hon. member that he has our good wishes and our heartiest congratulations.

That a select committee of the house be appointed to study and report upon the general problems of reconstruction and reestablishment which may arise at the termination of the present war, and all questions pertaining thereto; with power to such select committee to appoint, from among the members of the committee, such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable or necessary, to deal with specific phases of the problems aforementioned, with power to said select committee and to such subcommittees as may be formed therefrom, to call for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and for such select committee to report from time to time to the house; and that the said committee shall consist of the following members:	Messrs.
