maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, outside matters having to do with the carrying on of the war, the appointment of this committee is the most important matter that can come before us at this session of parliament. The business of providing for the war effort itself and the work of preparing plans for the post-war period are simply two parts of the same problem. The committee which sat last year has not, as far as I can learn, made any recommendations to parliament. I believe that was a disappoints ment to the people throughout the country because they expected that the committee would bring in important recommendations which would help us to plan our economic and social life when this war is over. They were looking for something better than we had between the end of the last war and the beginning of this one.
My purpose in speaking this afternoon is not to criticize the minister under whose auspices this motion is made and this work comes; rather it is, if I can, to assist him by impressing upon the members of this house the importance of the work indicated in the motion before us. There are people who believe that all plannings of this kind should be left until the war is over; indeed1 there are two schools of thought in the country in regard to it.
One school is composed of those who say, "Let us get on with the war; let us defeat Hitler; nothing matters now but victory." I have no doubt that many such people have tried to get the ear of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). Members of parliament are receiving booklets
Post-War Reconstruction

and pronouncements along this line from many sources. However, there is as I say another school of thought which believes that the preparation of comprehensive plans for postwar problems now would be a help rather than a hindrance to our war effort. Such plans are bound to improve the morale of our people. On the other hand, the absence of such plans is certain to be a damper on the morale of our people. This second school also believes that there are other things besides victory that matter; that is, that a military victory is not enough.
The first school is not large but it is influential. It is composed of those in comfortable positions, those to whom the present system has been kind. Such people look backward, not forward. They are in deathly fear of any change because they believe that any change can be only detrimental to them. They are in mortal fear of social changes, and in a large measure it was this fear of social change that led us unwittingly into the present war. This school is satisfied with things as they are. They think that the proper thing to do when the war is over is to go back to the pre-war status quo as quickly as possible.
The second school of thought includes all forward-looking people, people who realize that the pre-war status quo does not exist, that it would be quite impossible to go back to it even if we wished. They are the people who see in this war something more than a war; they see it as a world-wide social revolution. I believe that in this group can be included the Prime Minister ( Mr. Mackenzie King), if I heard aright the statement he made during his speech on the address. In the same group we can include the President of the United States, who is insistent, that the consideration and preparation of post-war plans should be a part of our work to-day. In his address at the opening of congress this year, President Roosevelt said:
I have been told this is no time to speak of a better America after the war. I am told it is a great error on my part. I dissent. If this becomes a matter of national debate the people will know where I stand.
Nothing, I think, could show clearer than this statement where President Roosevelt stands on post-war planning.
As I said, people who believe that we should start planning now are the people who recognize that a military victory is not enough. They remember that we had a military victory in 1918. They also remember the few years of ruthless exploitation and world-wide speculation that followed the last war, and they also remember the years of hunger, of misery and
fMr. Maclnnis.]
of want. They do not want at the end of the present war to find us as unprepared as we were at the end of the last war. As a matter of fact, they are convinced, as I am convinced, that all that the common people got out of the last war is this war.
I want to tell the minister and hon. members that a great psychological change has taken place in the minds of our people since this war began. I may be asked what has caused that change. I think I can state the reasons as they appear to me very briefly.
First, the people see that money in abundance can be found for war, and they are asking, if money can be found for war, for destruction, why cannot money be found just as easily for the creation of wealth and the creation of health and comfort?
Second, they see that to-day, although we have in the armed forces approximately 700,000 men and women who are not producing at all, and in war industries some 900,000 who are producing but are not producing consumers' goods, not producing wealth, nevertheless the people of Canada are at the present time better fed and better clothed than they were at any time between 1929 and 1939. They are asking why this should be. They are asking why it is that we are fearful of what may happen when peace comes, when to-day, with 1,600,000 men and women taken out of active production, our people are enjoying a better standard of living than perhaps they ever enjoyed before.
Third, the people of Canada have been tremendously impressed, as have the people of the whole world, by the military achievements of the Soviet Union. They had been told by all of the best people that a planned economy could not work. Yet they have seen a practical demonstration of the fact that a planned economy does work. They may not see all its implications, any more than you or I, Mr. Speaker, can see them all; nevertheless the fact remains that a planned economy does work, and our men and women will demand that they do not come back to the anarchy in production that they left when they went into the armed forces. The men and women in the armed forces expect that Canada will have a new deal ready for them when they come back. And not only do the men and women in the armed forces expect that. The workers in our war industries, the workers in our forests, the workers in our mines, the workers in our fisheries, the workers on our farms, expect that Canada will have a new deal, a new plan ready for them when this war is over.
If we do not begin now to prepare those plans, if we do not show the people that we

Post-War Reconstruction
are doing something now; if we do not give them tangible evidence of our sincerity in the matter, then there can be only one result. They will grow hopeless; they will become cynical; they will become defeatists; and when people get into that state, their minds become a fertile soil for every sort of screwball idea that may be offered to them.
A few days ago it was said in this chamber that the fall of France was caused by the multiplicity of the political parties which had grown up in that country. But that is a very superficial view of the situation in France in 1940. What caused the multiplicity of political parties? France fell so easily as a result of the greed of a few at the top, and the hopelessness and cynicism, and lack of faith of the masses of the people in their own ability to do anything. What the government of this country must do is not just to prepare plans but to take the people of Canada into its confidence and with their cooperation begin to make plans for the manifold problems which will confront us when this war is over. I suggest to the Minister of Pensions and National Health that he hurry the preparation of such plans with all possible speed.
I quote a short paragraph from a speech made by a great statesman, General Jan Christian Smuts, on June 28, 1919, at the signing of the treaty of Versailles.
Our allied peoples must remember that God gave them overwhelming victory, victory far beyond their greatest dreams, not for small, selfish ends, not for financial or economic advantages, but for the attainment of the great human ideals for which our heroes gave their lives, and which are the real factors in this war of ideals.
We should begin now to prepare plans which will indicate to the men and women in our armed forces that we appreciate the ideals for which they are prepared to give their lives, and that we shall not allow the victory which they will win for us on the military front to be debased to selfish ends.
As I mentioned before, the servants of privilege are already busy planning. Anything which the government of Canada will do will be done openly; everybody will know that we are doing it. But the plans of big business are generally formulated in secret. I have in my hands a page from the Financial Post of December 26, 1942. In it is an article by Horace T. Hunter, President of the Maclean Publishing Company Limited. In regard to post-war planning he has this to say:
The war has given private enterprise what may be its last chance to prove itself.
If private enterprise fails 'when the crisis comes-and that will be after the war-it will be replaced.
Replaced by what? Nobody knows. Bureaucracy, governmental control and ownership, confusion and chaos seem likely answers.
Horace T. Hunter of course assumes that private enterprise has not already failed. If private enterprise did not fail between 1929 and 1939, what was it that failed? He goes on:
Realization that this crisis lies ahead is driving the leading businesses of the United States into a brand new field of economies- postwar planning.
So important do these corporations regard the field of post-war planning that some of them are assigning vice-presidents and other officials to research on this task as a full-time job.
The researchers are faced with stupendous problems. _ They must get business away from its too individualistic past. They must prepare to assume leadership and coordination of effort on major questions. They must see to it that private enterprise has a broader conception of its duty to the community. They know that they cannot dream of returning to the thirty or forty per cent production which pertained in the 193'0's.
Mr. Hunter did not tell us why thirty to forty per cent production obtained in the 'thirties. He stated a fact without giving reasons, but the same reasons will apply in the 'forties, if we are lucky enough to finish the war during that period; it will apply at any time under the present system. Thirty and forty per cent production was inevitable because private enterprise, if you want to call it that-it is not that to-day; it is corporate enterprise-is not interested in industry as the means of producing the largest possible quantity of consumers' goods; it is interested in profit; and production was limited to thirty and forty per cent in order to reduce the amount of goods available and to maintain prices.
An hon. member undertook to tell the house the other day why Roosevelt's new deal policies failed. He said it was because the President, not satisfied with promoting public works and that sort of thing, went into various kinds of private business. But the hon. gentleman who told us that did not tell us that Roosevelt did not take office until March, 1933. He did not tell us that between 1929 and 1933 the whole economy of the United States had come to a standstill and business men were praying for someone to come along and start the wheels of industry going. Oh, yes, if you interfere with business you will destroy confidence! In one October day in 1929 on the New York stock exchange fourteen billion dollars, it is said, were lost. What destroyed confidence then? Private business never had such a free hand. But that is the inevitable result of anarchy.

Post-War Reconstruction

I want to bring the house a little nearer home. There came into my hands a few days ago the report of the Canadian Pacific Air Lines on business in the first year of operation. This report appeared in the Montreal Gazette of January 2, and is by L. B. Unwin, President of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. He mentions that in 1942, the first year of operation, Canadian Pacific Air Lines flew approximately six million scheduled aeroplane miles. Air cargo reached, he says, the record total of close to ten million pounds, and consisted largely of military and air defence shipments; in fact, ninety per cent of the total traffic handled by Canadian Pacific Air Lines was in connection with the war effort. Then he says:
In addition to its transport operations the company is the largest single civilian organization connected with the British commonwealth air training plan and operates, on a non-profit basis, six of a total of nine air observer schools, and one elementary flying training school.
This is significant, because for a year _ or more after the beginning of the war Canadian Pacific Air Lines was not in the air travel business at all and was not operating any schools, either observer or flying schools. He goes on.
It also manages five engine overhaul and aircraft repair plants under contract to the Department of Munitions and Supply lor the overhaul and repair of R.C.A.F. equipment. These establishments are spread across Canada and combined with the air transport services, are providing the nation with indispensable &iv facilities so necessary for the prosecution of a successful war effort.
I will now read the last paragraph of this significant report:
While the airplane to-day is an integral part of our war-time mechanism, it should not be overlooked that commercial aviation is destined to play a major role in reshaping a post-war world. In this regard the Canadian Pacific, as a long-established world-wide transport system, will undoubtedly through the extension of its air operations take its natural place in the development of world trade and travel routes to meet the almost unpredictable demands of the coming air age.
Here is a private company that has obtained control of a business that developed solely out of the country's war effort; and after the war we shall have this additional vested interest in our transport system with which to deal, just as we had another vested interest that prevented a solution of our transportation problems previously.
I want to say a few words in regard to this "private enterprise" about which we hear so much. No doubt those people who are so much afraid of government interference will approach the minister and, as I said before, try to get him to go slow with anything in the way
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
of national planning by the federal government. I would advise him not to listen to any blandishments of that kind. If he will read the speech delivered by his leader, Canada's Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), to the American Federation of Labor on October 9, 1941, I think he will find plenty of justification for going ahead with preparations of plans that will prevent chaos at the end of the war. I should like to quote two or three short paragraphs from the Prime Minister's speech. If hon. gentlemen opposite have not read it, I would suggest that they do so. If they have read it already, I would suggest that they read it again. The right hon. gentleman said:
I believe the war is teaching us that the obstacles to full employment were not real obstacles; that a partnership of management, of workers and of the community can make useful work available, in time of peace no less than in time of war, for all who need or want to work.
I should like to call attention to the words, " not real obstacles," and to the statement that the obstacles to full employment were not real. If they were not real obstacles they were phoney obstacles, and by his own words the Prime Minister has convicted himself of allowing phoney obstacles to stand in the way of full employment in this country at least from 1936 up to the beginning of the war. Then he went on:
But the work of repairing and restoring the ravages of war will not be enough. Fortunately, we are also learning that the only limit to our productive capacity is the limit of our resources, and our will and skill to use them to satisfy human need instead of human greed.
I should like to ask hon. members opposite if they think private enterprise, operating to make profits for shareholders, will have in mind "that the only limit to productive capacity is the limit of our resources, and our skill and will to use them to satisfy human need instead of human greed?" If you are going to leave the economy of this country on the old basis, which do you think will come first- human need or private greed? There is no doubt at all about the answer to that question. The answer has always been the same and will continue to be the same.
I have just one other quotation from the Prime Minister's speech. I am going to all this trouble because I am not sure that my hon. friends opposite have read it:
The war has shown us that the way of monopoly, of unrestricted power, is a way that leads to destruction, desolation and death. The only path of prosperity and of peace is, I believe, the path of equality, of cooperation, and of human brotherhood.
Well, do you think you can get equality, cooperation and human brotherhood from the

Post-War Reconstruction
people who are using the newspapers so freely to advertise differences between themselves and their employees; from people who vilify persons and groups who attempt to organize the workers; from people who under no circumstances will allow their employees a voice, not in the management of the industry, but even in determining the conditions under which they will sell their labour?
I want to quote a few short paragraphs from one of the most widely reviewed books on economics that has come to my notice for a long time. The book is entitled, " Conditions of Peace," and the author is Edward Hallett Carr, professor of international politics in the university college of Wales. I understand he is also an editorial writer on the London Times. In the two or three quotations that I am going to give he deals with the question of individualism and collectivism. He shows clearly that if ever there was any such thing as private enterprise it no longer exists. On page 71 he says:
The classical economists presupposed a society of independent, fully enlightened and completely mobile individuals, each- acting for himself, possessed of equal bargaining power, and equally interested in the economic system as producers and consumers. This hypothesis was never even approximately realized.
He continues:
The hypothesis of a vast society of equal, independent and mobile individuals was falsified to an ever-increasing extent. The individual counted less and less. The forces which dominated production and distribution and exercised a preponderant influence in the economic "society" were a few highly organized interest-groups, growing ever larger and more powerful. What is commonly referred to "individual enterprise" has been destroyed not, as its advocates sometimes pretend, by "socialism" or by the interference of grandmotherly governments but by the innate trend of competitive capitalism towards monopoly.
What have the advocates of private enterprise to say to that? One more quotation:
The issue miscalled individualism v. collectivism is not really the question whether economic enterprise should be controlled by the federal government or by men like Mr. Ford, but whether it should be controlled by a corporation responsible to the federal government or by some other equally collective, but not responsible, organization such as General Motors, Bethlehem Steel or Southern Utilities. "The choice ... is not between competition and monopoly, but between a monopoly which is irresponsible and private and a monopoly which is responsible and public."
That is the alternative, not only for this government but for every government in every democratic country in the world. So-called private enterprise no longer exists. We have corporate enterprise, which is an altogether different thing, controlling ever larger and 72537-45}
larger aggregates of capital, so that ultimately they control governments. With these facts before us may we not at this time go ahead in earnest to prepare the plans that are necessary to meet those problems which will confront us after the war?
Before taking my seat I should like to quote one more short paragraph from this book. Mr. Carr ends his book with this:
The old world is dead. The future lies with those who can resolutely turn their back on it and face the new world with understanding, courage and imagination.
Now, just a last word to the minister and to those who will be with him on the committee. When this war is over either we shall be ready with a plan, some sort of a planned economy, or we shall have turmoil, planned and unplanned.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow in the vein of the hon. member (Mr. Maclnnis) who preceded me. During all the days of my working manhood I was associated with that devoted portion of our population known as the working class. I was glad to belong to them. I am happy indeed that after perhaps twenty years as a worker in industry I can say I never in that time came in contact with the type of employer to Which the hon. member referred. The men with whom I came in contact were Christian gentlemen who spent their lives in trying to build up this country. I knew many of them who, year in and year out, did not receive a dollar on the investments they had; and I knew many more who delighted beyond measure in foregoing their profits, so that the companies with which they were associated could increase their size and thereby give more jobs. All my working life I have been one of those who have been firmly devoted to doing what I could to provide men with employment. I am one who believes that God intended that men and women born to this life should, in the days in which they were able to work, have an opportunity to do so, and that they should have that opportunity at a remuneration sufficient not only to take care of themselves and their families but to provide a competence for their older days. I am convinced of that.
So that to-night, while I rise to support the motion of the minister, what I have to say will be in reference to giving jobs. The reso-

all over adjacent land in the county of Kent and right up on to the main streets of Chatham and Thamesville. That occurred in 1937. But mark you, Mr. Speaker, in the flood of 1937 the crests of the floods on the north and south branches of the river did not synchronize. The south branch of the river rose to the colossal flow of 43-03 cubic feet per second per square mile of watershed, and it overflowed the whole course of that branch of the river. Had the crest on the north branch of the river synchronized with the crest on the south branch, the whole of south London might have been wiped out. As it was, the whole of south London was under several feet of water. I do know how many people, if any, were drowned in that flood; but I do know that every farm, every village and every hamlet west of London along the river suffered grievously. Had the crests of the floods on the two branches of the river synchronized, it would have made a flood of 47-033 cubic feet per second flowing through south London, and space is not there to take care of that volume of water. Why should the minister not have his engineers commence making surveys at once and a programme outlined for flood-proofing the Thames river which flows through a very rich and thickly settled country? That is one project which I recommend. Whether the committee will be able to recommend specific projects I do not know. I hope the minister will see that the committee is given the power to make specific concrete recommendations of projects at which men can be put to work. The Thames floodproofing could be done at a cost of $1,600,000 and would provide four months work for three thousand men. That would be a very nice start at least, and would help to take up the slack. That is only one river. There are many others where flood-proofing and improvement work could be done.
I will mention one other little river, the Ganaraska river, in the county of Durham. It has a pretty small watershed of ninety square miles, but a tremendous amount of water can flow over that area. I have seen the Ganaraska overflow right up to the St. Lawrence hotel on the main street in the town of Port Hope, and that is quite a distance. It flowed over the whole lower end of the town of Port Hope and caused a vast amount of damage. The same with the Etobicoke in the riding of my hon. friend the member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). In his riding is the substantial town of Brampton, than which there is no more beautiful town in the whole province. But that fine town stands in jeopardy every day of the spring through the 
possible overflowing of the Etobicoke river. I have seen that river, as my hon. friend has, flow down the main street of Brampton. The overflowing hitherto has been caused by the melting of snow and ice. They have never yet had a cloudburst there. If they had one the damage would be colossal. The watershed north of Brampton has an area of twenty-five square miles that could produce over 160,000,000 cubic feet of water in a flood like that which took place at Fond du Lac,. and there is no place in the river bed at Brampton for that volume of water to pass through.
I will leave with the minister for his consideration the suggestions I have made for a programme of flood-proofing the rivers that flow through our fine towns and cities. It would be a means of providing a large amount of employment, and it would be self-liquidating work. All the figures with respect to the Grand river, for instance, could be readily obtained by the minister through the responsible department, and they could tell at once how many men were employed in improving the Grand watershed.
I want to make another suggestion. I was away up on the Slave river, and at Fort Fitzgerald we were invited to get out of the boat and make a portage of eighteen miles to Fort Smith. Canada has possessed that area ever since 1870. What have we done for it since 1870? As far as I can see, not a single, solitary mortal thing as to improved navigation. There is quite a considerable amount of traffic down that river, up to 50,000 tons during the summer months, and if the river were cleaned out and the traffic speeded up, there is no reason why the tonnage would not increase materially. That is one place where we could build a marine railway. The same applies to the Peace river at Vermilion chutes. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons) goes there every summer to see his constituents and he is well aware of what I am speaking. From Hudson Hope on the Peace river to Vermilion chutes is about 600 miles, and from there to where the river flows into the Slave river is another 300 miles. There are 900 miles of a magnificent river flowing through the riding of the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Turgeon), the riding of the hon. member for Peace River and on to the Slave. The only obstruction in that whole distance of 900 miles is that little bit of obstruction at Vermilion chutes, which is not over four miles long, counting in the falls and the rapids. Why could men not be sent to canal around that obstruction? It is a job that has waited ever since 1870. If this work were done and a canal on the Slave were constructed, boats could sail from Hudson Hope right down to

Posl-War Reconstruction
Aklavik, a distance of nearly 3000 miles. Here is a chance to do something which in the end. would cost this country nothing, because it would open up that great country which is filled to overflowing with incomparable resources the like of which is to be found nowhere else in the world.
One further thought and I will close. I said a moment ago that I have been through the riding of my hon. friend the member for Cariboo. I went as far west last summer as Hudson Hope and a little bit further. I hope that he will urge as strongly as he can, and I will support him, that a roadway be built on the north side of the Peace river right through his riding so that traffic can pass on the north side of the Peace river all the way through to connect with the roadway to Prince Rupert. That would require the opening of a road from Fort St. John to Hudson Hope, to Bullhead mountain, where the great coal mine is, and past Goldbar to Manson Creek. I hope the chairman of the committee will be able to persuade the committee to recommend the construction of these and similar projects which will provide work for quite a large number of men and will not cost the country anything because they will be self-liquidating projects. That is only one road.
I do not want to prolong my remarks. But flood proofing, the building of roads, and, perhaps, assistance to navigation can all be done as government works, and all, in my judgment, are self-liquidating. All would require a great deal of labour and would employ men with various kinds of training- engineers, concrete mixers, builders, carpenters, drivers, truck drivers, those who make cement, those who make the steel which enters into construction, etcetera. The ramifications are almost endless. That in my judgment would be a plan to follow.
I have tried to lift the debate a little by presenting something concrete. I am here for only one purpose, to try to help this country, and for nothing else. There is nothing in it for me personally. But while I am here I want to lift my voice at all times on behalf of projects which will provide jobs for the multitude to whom I belong, the forking class. Consideration for them comes first with me, because I have been with them, worked with them, and know them. I have shared their joys and their sorrows; and there are no finer people in the world.
I offer these few thoughts as suggestions to the minister. If he views them favourably I should appreciate it very much if he would instruct the chairman of the committee-and wre have a good chairman-to bring in concrete, definite proposals. That is the only thing in the resolution which I am not sure has been made clear, and if there is any doubt I should like to have it clarified. I want definite directions to the chairman to bring in concrete proposals, so that when the war ceases, plans will be ready to send five hundred men here, a thousand men there, and to notify this contractor and that producer to have this and that ready.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I am glad that the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment has been appointed in the early days of the session, because I am of opinion that our plans for post-war reconstruction should be pushed at this time with the utmost vigour. If the united nations can convince the peoples of occupied Europe of our sincerity as regards a new order and a new world, this may help materially to shorten the war. Our reason for pushing forward plans at this time should be two-fold; first, to reassure the people of Europe that we are sincere when we talk of a new world; and, second, that we may be ready at the end of the war 'to move from a war-time to a peace-time economy as smoothly as possible.
I hope that it may be possible at this session for the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment to come to grips with the real problems which confront us. In the past this committee has dealt with a number of very interesting points. We dealt, for instance, with the question of nutrition, and we were told by Dr. Thomson of McGill university that if the people of this country were given a balanced diet it would be possible greatly to increase the consumption of agricultural products; I think he said we could double the consumption of many of them. An interesting point in that regard is that we were perfectly well aware in the years from 1935 to 1939 that if the Canadian people were to have a balanced diet it would be necessary to increase their consumption of agricultural products. We have the agricultural products, but we did not take steps at that time to make that balanced diet available to the people; and in the committee we did not discuss ways and means by which that balanced diet might be made available, whereby it might be possible for the people of Canada to secure those products. For it is not merely the unemployed who are in that position; there are great numbers of people in this country in the low income brackets who are suffering from a low standard of living.
We also discussed at some length the development of the resources of this country:
Post-War Reconstruction

it was a very interesting subject. To me the main point of interest is, what will you do with your increased production resulting from the increased development of your resources? How will you market the increased production from the increased development of those resources? That has been the problem of the past and that, undoubtedly, will be the main problem of the future.
We knew in the past-we knew in the depression years-that Canada possesses great resources which could be developed. We had the unemployed available, but we did not develop those resources. Why? Because we knew very well that, if we did, we would not be able to sell the resulting production.
In my opinion it is nonsense to talk about full employment unless at the same time ways and means are found to market the increased production resulting from that increased employment. No industry can continue to expand its production unless at the same time it can expand its markets. That has been the problem of the past. That was the main problem of all industrialized nations up to the beginning of this war. It was especially the problem of Canada from the last war up to the beginning of the present one, especially from 1930 to 1939. During that period we had industries running at only a small percentage of their capacity. There were hundreds of thousands of unemployed; yet industry could1 not sell its limited production. At the same time over a million people were on relief, and in that million we had a great potential market. They represented a physical demand, but a physical demand cannot absorb goods unless it is backed up by money. In other words, that demand was not an effective demand and therefore industry was not in a position to expand its production.
That problem, I think everyone will agree, was national and internal. Unfortunately the government refused to recognize it as such and tried to internationalize it by dumping it on the doorstep of other nations. I say that for this reason. From 1935 to 1939 this country maintained on an average a favourable balance of payments amounting to $218,000,000 annually, the idea being no doubt that the money paid out in the production of that wealth which was exported abroad and for which we accepted no imports 'in return would help to maintain an effective demand against the production of the country which was left, internally.
My greatest condemnation of a policy of this kind is that there can be no justification for exporting more wealth out of the country than you import at the same time that you 
have hundreds of thousands of people in your country in a state of destitution, as we had from 1935 to 1939, when a million were on relief.
I should like to quote from a statement made by the London chamber of commerce in this regard. I have here a copy of the report put out by the chamber on "General Principles of a Post-War Economy." It is dated May 12, 1942. The London chamber of commerce has a direct membership of nine thousand firms and an approximate affiliated membership of fifty thousand; it is probably the greatest organization of its kind to be found anywhere in the world. This is what they have to say regarding the practice of maintaining a favourable balance of trade in payments. I want to quote sections 19 to 21, which read:
19.	If some nations have "favourable" balances it necessarily follows that others have "unfavourable" ones. The successful nations get others into unpayable debt. The reward of success being power over other nations, and the penalty for failure economic servitude, the struggle for a "favourable" balance has largely obscured, in the eyes of the nations, the real purpose of international trade. It has accordingly degenerated into a desperate financial war.
20.	It is an obvious absurdity that nations should regard it as necessary to export their real wealth, not for the purpose of paying for imports, but in order to solve their domestic unemployment problem by passing it on to other countries. Exports with this end in view are nothing more nor less than an excuse for distributing wages to people who otherwise would be unemployed. This purpose would be equally well served if the goods were to be thrown into the sea or if the people were to be employed to dig holes and to fill them up again.
21.	When, however, it is remembered that even wealthy nations have a large percentage of their population under-fed, ill-clothed and ill-housed, it is clear that these would be the best recipients of this alleged surplus wealth. What is necessary is to improve the technique for the internal provision of money, so as to convert this human demand into effective demand.
That used to be England's policy prior to the last great war, and it was Canada's policy prior to the present war. In the foreword to this report it is interesting to note that consideration that was given to the framework within which the work of reconstruction should be carried on. I think the committee of this house might very well take this matter into consideration also. The foreword reads:
A special committee was appointed by the council of the London chamber of commerce, on the 10th March, 1942, to consider and report on post-war reconstruction. That special committee took the view that it could not usefully consider the many secondary problems which would arise, both in the period of transition from war to peace and in the subsequent period, without first ascertaining the view of the council

Post-War Reconstruction
upon. the framework within which the future economic system should be built. The special committee therefore submitted the enclosed preliminary report dealing with these questions of major policy.
The report was received and adopted by the council at its meeting on the 12th May, 1942, and the special committee was congratulated and requested to make a further report on the assumption that the detailed problems which will face the nation at the end of hostilities will call for solution within the framework here envisaged.
Just what is the framework within which our committee will work? For instance, does anyone really believe that this new social order can be built on the foundation of a debt-creating capitalistic" system? If anyone believes there is any possible chance of building a new world on that basis I think it might be well for him to remember the words of the general manager of the bank of Montreal back in 1938. This is what Mr. Spinney said at that time:
Canada's debt burden is gradually lowering the general standard of living.
Since the beginning of the war the rate of growth, of our debt has been greatly accelerated, and by the end of the war our debt will be very much greater than it was at the time Mr. Spinney made that statement. The burden of the debt in 1938 was such as to lower the standard of living of the Canadian people. How much greater will be the danger of our debt lowering the standard of living after the war, when our debt will have reached a far greater figure. The danger will be that at the end of the war expenditures will be restricted to meet debt charges, at the very time when expenditures should be made in order to meet the needs of post-war reconstruction. I was very much interested in a dispatch which appeared in the press to-day concerning a discussion that took place in the House of Lords, where the Beveridge report was being discussed. One of the lords, a former Canadian, opposed the Beveridge report on the ground that at the end of this war England's debt in all probability will have reached the sum of one hundred billion dollars, and that the first charge against the wealth of England would be the interest charged on that debt. That is something which we might well keep in mind in this country, because there will be plenty of people, even right in this house, who will talk about the sacredness of the written contract and will suggest that the first charge against our production at the end of the war must be the interest charged on the debt we are accumulating to-day.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I say that if we are going to build a new world order it must be upon a firmer foundation than a debt-72537-46
creating system such as we have had in the past, which is putting us under a burden of unpayable debt, which in turn will bring forth retorts such as the one I have just mentioned. Consequently I believe, as the London chamber of commerce states, that before you can sit down and give any serious consideration to a problem like post-war reconstruction, you must know the framework within which you are operating. That is why several times in the committee last year I said I felt that we were floundering, that we were travelling a road which went we knew not where, and that we did not know how we were going to travel it. In my opinion, first of all we should decide upon our objective; then we should decide upon the main obstacles to achieving that objective, and finally we should decide upon the ways and means of removing those obstacles. That was the way in which we always dealt with, problems in the army in the last war, and I suppose that is the way in which problems are dealt with in the army in this war, but no doubt that is altogether too direct an approach for this government to take.
What is our objective? Many people say that our objective to-day is full employment; yet the same people will disagree as to the purpose of that full employment. I see the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) is in his seat. I do not doubt for one moment that he would say the purpose of full employment is to put everyone at work and guarantee them a subsistence allowance. Supposing we had a steam shovel, requiring six men to operate it, and in the same vicinity we had another twenty men who were idle. I do not doubt that the hon. member for Brant would advocate that we should set the steam shovel to one side and put the twenty-six men at work with picks and shovels and wheelbarrows in order to give them employment, and pay them a subsistence allowance. I say I do not doubt the hon. member for Brant would agree to that, because that was the attitude he adopted toward the agricultural problem two years ago. He criticized the farmers for operating tractors and said they should go back to horses. We could put everyone at work if we scrapped modem machinery; if they did too much work with shovels we could give them teaspoons instead, and certainly then we could put everyone to work. But I say that is a nonsensical approach and one which must be entirely discredited. Any time you start to put aside the advances of science in the form of great machines, you begin to lower the standard of living of the people. We want to use all the machines we have and all our man-power to run those machines, for the express purpose of giving

everyone an optimum standard of living. Therefore I would say that full employment must be for the purpose of providing an optimum standard of living for the people. If our objective is optimum production rather than full employment then we shall have to use modern machines, and not do as we did during the depression. On many occasions I saw from twenty to forty men cutting down hillsides when steam shovels were available in the vicinity. I have seen men put at digging ditches just in order to put the men to work when a digging machine was there to do the work. That is why I am so bitterly opposed to anyone saying that our objective is to put everyone to work. That is not our objective at all; the objective is to provide everyone in the country with the highest possible standard of living.
What are the main obstacles in the way of achieving that objective? On account of certain practices inherent in the capitalistic system industry does not and cannot maintain an effective demand for its own production, except in times of abnormal capital goods construction such as in war time, such as we have to-day. In proof of that, although I need not give any proof, I quote from a national survey of potential production of the United States, 1934-35, under the Hoover administration, under the chairmanship of Doctor Harold Loeb. He wrote a book entitled "A Chart of Plenty", dealing with this report. At page 71 there appears this statement:
The total national monetary income in 1929 did not equal the total price asked for the goods which could have been produced by the plant then existing. But instead of dropping prices until monetary income was able to command full production (which is the classical answer to this situation), prices were maintained and production was restricted. Consequently, national monetary income did not in 1929, nor does it to-day, command the full production of our industrial plant. Which is another way of saying that the national income was not what . it should have been. In fact, since 1929, the national monetary income has been commanding an ever-decreasing volume of consumer goods and the actual national income has become but a fraction of the possible national income.
Then on page 78 he says:
The whole problem really comes down to the first proposal-in other words, to buying pow'er. At present, production is curtailed to meet a grossly inadequate buying-power. An efficiently managed society would consciously and scientifically adjust its economic mechanisms so that buying power would always command full desirable production.
I do not want to spend much time in dealing with the cause of that situation. In passing, I might say it is quite obvious that since the machine has displaced men the wages that used

to be paid to the men are now being paid to the owners of the machine, and the incomes of the machine owners have become so great that they cannot spend their total incomes. Also the practice of charging profits into prices without distributing the wherewithal to pay it and the practice of paying old debts out of current income-all these things cause lack of purchasing power. I do not want to take time to go into those matters in detail. But I say that as a result of that there has not been maintained in this country or in any of the capitalistic nations an effective demand against the production of the country; and unless you have an effective demand against the production you are bound to curtail production.
I wish to discuss for a few minutes ways and means by which that obstacle can be overcome. If we are prepared to admit that our main objective is optimum production, and that the main obstacle to achieving that objective is tack of effective demand, then obviously the solution is in equating demand to supply instead of, as in the past, trying to reduce supply to demand. Doctor Loeb puts it quite simply on page 161 of his report when he states:
It would seem that a simple and obvious way out, that of giving buying power adequate to procure desired goods and services to the limit of our ability to produce them might well be tried. It is simple in principle but has not been attempted.
The London chamber of commerce in the report to which I have already referred also deals with this problem in sections 24 and 25:
24.	After the last war there was more skilled labour in the world, more capital equipment, and more developed sources of raw material than at the beginning. The w-orld was therefore potentially richer. Instead, however, of equating effective demand with supply-even using it to stimulate supply-capital equipment was scrapped, the output of raw material limited or destroyed, and millions of men were prevented from producing; in some eases they were paid not to produce.
25.	Instead of trying to equate supply with effective demand, the chamber advocates that, in future, effective demand should be equated with supply. There can be no such thing as general over-production, of which complaint was made after the last war, although of course there can be over-production of a particular commodity in relation to others. The real trouble is underconsumption.
With a view to preparing plans for the post-war period a conference was held at Edmonton last December. At that conference the following resolution was passed dealing with the subject to which I have just referred.

On post-war reconstruction.
