maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
A general meeting was called, everyone being invited to it; people from different classes, farmer and labour organizations etcetera were invited. This is a resolution passed at that conference:
1.	That a complete survey should be made forthwith to ascertain the nature and volume of the products of industry which will be required by the Canadian people following the war to rehabilitate themselves, and to raise their standard of living to the level which our natural resources can consistently maintain.
2.	That a complete survey of Canadian war industries be made to determine the adaptability of each to the production of those peace-time requirements, and to plan and prepare the steps necessary to bring about that conversion in each case at the end of the war.
3.	That a survey be made of the possible foreign markets which may be available at the end of the war, and the part which Canadian industry should play in the rehabilitation of those countries whose industries have been destroyed or disorganized as a result of the war.
I suggest that surveys of that kind should be conducted in a very similar way to the way in which the national survey of the potential product capacity of the United States was conducted under the Hoover administration. Because that survey disclosed two things; it showed not only what the production of the country could be, but also what the consumption of the country would in all probability be if the needs of the people were satisfied. Let me read the reference in that regard. On page 11 it is stated:
By such working back and forth we finally arrive at a close approximation of the quantity of goods and services (the budget) which the people of the United States might expect if production were directed towards the satisfaction of their needs and reasonable desires, and if production were limited only by physical factors and the "product capacity" of the existing plant.
But also, surprising as it may seem, the budget lists with fair accuracy the goods and services which the American people icould consume if their desires were satisfied! In other words, the budget is not only an estimate of possible production but also of possible consumption-excluding the assumption of a radical alteration in habits, such as would result if the practice of aeroplane joy-riding became general or if television sets came into popular, use.
Accordingly I am of opinion that before we can handle this question of post-war reconstruction in a really intelligent manner we should have surveys of that kind, and have that information majie available to us.
The United States in dealing with this took into consideration only physical factors. ' They did not take into consideration any form of financial restriction. One might say that has been the proclaimed policy of this government 72537-481
during this war, namely, that no financial restriction shall be allowed to impede our war effort.
I think the committee on post-war reconstruction should also receive a declaration from the government as to what its financial policy' is in regard to peace. Is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) prepared to say that no financial restriction of any kind shall be allowed to impede our peace effort? When this sqrvey was made in the United States, that was taken for granted. They took into consideration only physical obstacles, and did not take into account any monetary ones. This is what the committee found could be done in the United States:
After almost a year of research by sixty technicians financed by the federal government, the national survey of potential product capacity has released its findings. The results are briefly stated. If the existing plant and man-power in the United States were fully employed in the production of honest goods and services for the consumer the total output, valued in 1929 dollars would not he less than $135,000,000,000 or an average per family of approximately $1,400.
That was in 1935. Since that time the productive plant of the United States has been considerably increased. Therefore if it w7as possible in 1935 to provide for a family in the United States a standard of living of $4,400, how much greater could the standing of living be after this war? Consequently I would say that at the end of the war our first problem will be to expand production of consumer goods as rapidly as possible, to satisfy the needs of the people, and then after that a definite relationship will have to be maintained between production of capital goods and production of consumer goods, so that the money paid out in capital goods industries is sufficient to make up any deficiency which may occur as between the total prices of the consumer goods and the effective demand against them.
When I refer to capital goods industries I use the expression in its widest term, so as to include various national projects. To-day during the war we have an abnormal expansion of capital goods and, of course, the result is inflationary. From 1930 to 1939 the production of capital goods in Canada was away down below normal and, as we know, during that period we had a deflationary condition. Therefore it is necessary for the government to assume full responsibility at all times for maintaining the correct relationship between the production of capital goods and the production of consumer goods.
In my opinion one of the most essential projects after the war will be a large-scale housing scheme. I do not mean a housing
Post-War Reconstruction

scheme such as we have had in the past, because under such schemes the people who were most in need of houses were unable to afford them. I should like to see a nationwide housing scheme which would make possible to people in the lowest income brackets the acquisition of decent housing. A scheme of that kind would have to be financed by the Bank of Canada and, in so far as interest is concerned, it should be at the actual cost of servicing the accounts. Money should be repaid only at the rate of depreciation of the houses. That is to say, if a loan were made to a man to build a house estimated to last thirty years, such loan should be repaid in thirty annual instalments, so that when the house had completely depreciated the loan would be paid off. In this way a person would be able to build a house for much less than he could rent one, because the interest, apart from the actual cost of handling the accounts, would be cut off.
I believe this would be especially desirable at the end of the war. Soldiers needing houses will be returning. Workers will be moving from the cities to the more decentralized portions of the country, and they, too, will be needing houses. Generally speaking, those people will not be in a position to afford houses under housing schemes such as we have had in the past.
Before concluding my remarks I should like to refer to one or two other aspects of postwar reconstruction. For instance, there is the vexed problem of international trade. So long as we maintain an effective demand against our production, international trade will be simply an exchange of goods as between nations. There will be no incentive to maintain a favourable balance, of trade, as we have in the past because, as the London chamber of commerce has pointed out, that has been brought about by a lack of effective demand within the country.
So far as our share of helping to take care of the blitzed areas is concerned, I believe Canada must be prepared to make her contribution along with other nations, and to make that contribution in the form of a gift. Of course to that extent the standard of living of the people would be reduced. But as soon as the nations of the world become rehabilitated and are able to stand on their own feet we must be prepared to trade with them on an even basis, exchanging goods for goods.
I believe the suggestion put forward by the Lbndon chamber of commerce with respect to foreign trade is a good one. We should be willing to exchange our goods for the goods of other countries on an even

basis; and if any nation refuses to accept goods in payment of its exports, then over a period of time its credit should be cancelled. All a debtor nation can do is to offer its goods in payment for its imports. If the creditor nation will not accept those goods, then the only thing to do is to cancel the debt,, rather than to allow the debtor nation to be forced into unpayable debts. Such a programme of course would entail definite control of industry, and in my opinion would necessitate the nationalization of the whole banking system.
On the other hand, of course, if the government is going to insist upon carrying on under the financial policy it has followed before, then I believe that the work of the committee to a great extent will be in vain.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the committee to be appointed will have before it a great task, and I wish the government of the day and those hon. members on the committee every success in their work. In the first place, the war is still. far from being won. We are at the darkest hour. The allies-they are called the united nations; one seldom hears the name of Britain any more, although she is one of the pioneer nations-are now called the united nations, and they have just begun to take the initiative in Africa. Mr. Churchill says we are at the end of the beginning.
The whole of Europe is still dark. No one knows how long the war will last. Reconstruction and planning are international, national and domestic in scope. It is also linked with the war. The whole matter is inter-related. The first and second resolutions on the order paper are complementary, and might have been dealt with together. As a matter of fact they were considered together in the British House of Commons. Sir William Jowitt, paymaster-general, who has charge of this particular branch of legislation in the British government, presented legislation causing a twelve-day debate on the address in the British House of Commons, before the committee was appointed. They considered the war aspect, the international aspect, the empire [DOT]and domestic sides of the question and empire trade. And what did they show? Well, I am sorry the Prime Minister did not accept my suggestion offered a few days ago, namely, that we should have a separate debate of one day at least to chart out a similar course, because if we had I believe these two resolutions might have been taken together, and we might have saved time.
In the British House of Commons men took part who were home from the front. In the

Post-War Reconstruction
list' were admirals, airmen, generals in the army, and men who had a great deal to do with the last war, and now serve at the front in this one. They attempted to chart the course which they thought should be followed. There was a debate in the British House of Commons on reconstruction, rehabilitation and social security. The result was that when the Beveridge report w-as considered it was found to be a little too utopian for the mother country and I doubt if it ever will be adopted over there. It is not a practical report for this country because we have a different system. Our municipalities constitute a branch of government- there are the provincial governments constituting a- duplicate municipal system, and there is also the federal government. Under our constitution the Beveridge report could not be adopted.
One of the main things is to win the war. We can plan until doomsday, but we must first win the war. I think I had probably as much to do with reconstruction after the last war as any hon. member. There were a million and a quarter people in our district, and we provided for reconstruction with little or no aid from the federal government and little or no aid from the provincial authorities. The municipality of Toronto had to handle this work. A total of 58,000 soldiers returned to the district, and for a while the situation was intolerable. However, matters were straightened out through the activities of the local municipality.
The old city of Toronto extended from the waterfront as far as St. Clair avenue. A private company owned the street railway franchise, but the city took that over. They also bought all the radial railways entering the city and in 1921 started the Toronto transportation commission system, and under the so-called clean-up deal which entailed an expenditure of $33,000,000 for the companies power and transportation facilities were provided and power in the clean-up deal from the Niagara district. The harbour improvements and the work along the waterfront were carried out, a new station and viaduct started, and the new city had to be provided with schools, sewers, roadways and municipal institutions of all kinds. The result was that the provision of this reconstruction work aided in preventing a great unemployment disaster from occurring to that city.
There is bound to be a period of dislocation after every war. Neither victory nor any kind of planning can bring about the millen-ium. The same thing happened in the days of the Roman empire and the old Grecian empire. A description of those days will be found in Gibbon's "Decline and Fall of the
Roman Empire". Great things were to be done for the Roman soldiers, almost similar to what is proposed to-day. But after those wars all they had were circuses and doles and all that kind of thing, and the empire was almost destroyed.
We had the Napoleonic wars, the Crimean war, the South African war, the great war, and then this particular war. In spite of all the planning that was done after the last war this country did not become a land fit for heroes to live in. After the last war the soldiers were forgotten three months after they came home. Apart from the city I have mentioned, notwithstanding all the planning that was done, the soldiers received little or no consideration. The result is that to-day many from the last war are suffering untold hardships.
As Mr. Churchill said about this war, we have just reached the end of the beginning. No one knows how long it is going to last and we do not know to whom the country will belong. The Germans still control the whole of Europe. We have not got inside their defences, and with the exception of part of Russia they are in full control of that continent. I do not object to this planning; I wish the committee good luck, but I think we are putting the cart before the horse. We should first chart out the course we are going to pursue.
For example, what are we going to do about empire trade and about the mother country? I think the government should lay down its policy in this regard. The mother country has been our best customer and she has spent a fortune developing the colonial empire. Britain's colonial empire is, in many ways, an example of world reconstruction. One has only to read the speech of Lord Cranborne to realize what has been done in building up this colonial empire. The word "imperialism" is much misunderstood and much misinterpreted in this house. Our allies Russia and the United States are imperialistic; they may not be imperialistic in the sense of grabbing territory, although that remains to be seen when the peace terms are known. They are imperialistic in that they want a larger share in world affairs and will want to dominate the peace terms.
Our fine ally the United States with their great president will want to have a larger share in world affairs and reconstruction. In considering the reconstruction of the new world we shall have to decide one thing. All the planning in the world will not mean anything unless this is decided. What is to be our relationship with the mother country and

Post-War Reconstruction
the empire in empire trade, food and raw materials? The mother country saved civilization after Dunkirk. Only for her we wbuld have been forced to make peace with the axis. Yesterday I referred to Poland where virtually a million of the population have been taken to abattoirs to be killed by the gestapo. Notwithstanding what has been said elsewhere, I believe that after the war the United States will become an isolationist country. We must consider the international feature of this matter.
We come now to the domestic and national feature of this work. Since the war started, everybody has become a socialist or a planner. While we members of the House of Commons belong to different parties, there has been a fine spirit of sportsmanship shown in this chamber during the debates, and I have found the House of Commons to be a place of much kindness, with the possible exception of one or two cases. But everyone is proposing some sort of planning for the post-war period and the spending of our post-war incomes. I do not know whether we are going to have much in the way of post-war income. As I say, all the planning in the world will not bring about better days. With the billions of dollars that are being spent we may be a desperately poor nation after the war. We have been squandering our resources at a great pace; we have been spending money like water. One thing that must be settled is what is to be done with our soldiers when they come home. Do not forget that five or six hundred thousand soldiers will not, on their return, act merely as viewers of all this planning. We can plan until doomsday, but our soldiers who have gone overseas to fight for us, and have gone over there voluntarily and suffered three or four years of isolation in Britain, doing almost the work of labour battalions, will, on their return, have something to say about all this planning. The able minister is a returned soldier himself and has for years taken a great deal of interest in the soldiers and reconstruction. I submit to him and to the government that there should be a system of national insurance of our soldiers just as there is in the United States. A soldier's bill has passed both houses of congress protecting the soldier and his family and his property for three years after the war, and reestablishing him. It is a national system of insurance, which I have urged here since this war began.
Further, I believe that this committee might well consider many of the resolutions on the order paper dealing with reconstruction and rehabilitation problems. The official opposition and some of my hon. friends to my left have motions of that kind on the order paper, and 
this committee which is to deal with reconstruction might well have these resolutions referred to them. After all is said and done, we wasted almost four months last year on the plebiscite and Bill No. 80, to amend the mobilization act, and we had no time left to consider resolutions of hon. gentlemen to my left and of the official opposition and some good motions by private members on the government side. I suggest that these resolutions be referred to the committee.
One thing I should like to see Canada adopt is a national coal supply. This country is famished for coal at the present time, and conditions will get worse as the war goes on. I urged this policy before the house from 1923 on, for seven or eight years, and you, Mr. Speaker, when you first entered the house, coming as you do from the west and knowing well the conditions in the mining districts and in the municipalities which you have so long and faithfully represented in this house, took a great deal of interest in this policy of a national fuel supply. We have coal in Nova Scotia, Alberta and other parts of this country, and we could develop our resources so that we could provide ourselves with our own fuel.
We should also have a national policy of hydro development, and an oil development policy, involving the construction of pipelines. That policy was before the house in 1923 or 1924. We have a potential water-power supply of 43,000,000 horse-power, of which only one-seventh, or about 7,000,000 horse-power has so far been developed. The last time I was in British Columbia, in 1927, I was surprised that with the great natural resources of that province there was no hydro development. It is the same story on the prairies. My hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has taken a great interest in the water powers of this country and has visited many potential sites. Of that 7,000,000 horsepower which is developed at the present time, a considerable part is a seasonal development only. There has been an additional development since the war began, and I should like to see a further expansion. I think that is one matter which the committee might well consider.
I come to agriculture. There can be no proper agriculture without proper housing, and we are behind the times in housing. Housing is a suburban, urban and rural matter, and we have done little or nothing to develop a housing policy for Canada. In the Toronto district from which I come there will be no houses for the soldiers when they come back from the v ar unless action is taken. Some soldiers' families are now living in cellars. There is a great scarcity of adequate accommodation, and

Post-War Reconstruction
that is a matter which should be looked into by the committee. Urban, suburban and rural housing, reconstruction, and health and education legislation should also be considered.
The provision of raw materials is both a national and an international question. The mother country has to import twenty-five out of twenty-seven raw materials which she needs. She has coal and half her needs in iron, but the rest she has to import. Without an import and an export trade the mother country would become a second-class power. She would become a second Denmark and just an outpost at the edge of Europe for America, I believe in Mr. Churchill's policy which he announced in London, that he is not going to see this empire sold down the river, or go by default, but that Britain is going to hold what she has. It is our duty to work with our best customer, and to help her after the war, for we owe everything to her for having saved our shores from the enemy. Every country of the world has received raw materials from the colonial empire, because that has always been Britain's policy. Millions of dollars have been spent on the development of this colonial empire by Great Britain, and she has never asked for a dollar from them in return. She has made the raw materials of that colonial empire available to the whole world. As a publication of the League of Nations says, the colonial empire has given more in the way of raw materials to foreign countries than to the mother country which was responsible for the development of that empire, and has given the colonial empire preferences in her markets.
There is also the question of the development of civil aviation. In the last war the Royal Air Force had some eighteen thousand young men trained in military aeronautics in the city of Toronto. There was no Royal Canadian Air Force then. Montreal was considered by the government, but Toronto was finally chosen as the headquarters for the development of the Royal Air Force, and there eighteen thousand cadets and air mechanics were trained. Some two thousand United States students were among them. They came from various universities in the United States. After the war what happened? Colonel Barker, V.C., Collishaw, Bishop and others tried to persuade the government and the city of Toronto to take up civil aviation after the last war. But nothing was done. The result was that many of these young men who had been trained in military aeronautics here went to the United States after the war, and there a few of them got a nearly ninety
million dollar contract in California from the Chamberlain government in the early days of rearmament. If Canada and the other dominions are not alert, the development of civil aviation will fall into the hands of other countries after the war.
We hear a great deal these days about reconstruction. But the first thing this government will have to reestablish is private enterprise, as they are doing in England. There a resolution was moved by a former labour representative in the Churchill cabinet. The British parliament has passed an act known as the "Pre-War Trade Practices Act", to put back after the war the retail and wholesale trade where it was before the war. When the troops come home they will not have anybody like Mr. Donald Gordon here dominating them. They will have something to say about these bureaucrats. I have fought against these bureaucrats since the time of their appointment, and I was nearly all alone, except for the support, last session or two, of my hon. friend the former leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson, York-Sunbury). In Great Britain, within six months or a year after the war is over, they will go back to private enterprise and the old way of doing things. If we had had no bureaucrats, there would have been no scarcity of food and no rationing. I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is quite right. I pointed out .two years ago that we should have a food ministry. The food ministry in Britain under Lord Woolton has done magnificent work. Food supplies have been planned; the food is available to everyone, it is fresh, it is well handled, and there have been practically no complaints. A minister of the British government, Sir William Jowitt, paymaster general, referred to reconstruction plans which have already been prepared with relation to the food problem in the mother country. Britain has been the best customer of our farmers, not least of the grain growers of the prairies. Let us not lose her after the war. I believe that this dominion should immediately, through this committee, work with Mr. Churchill and his government along the lines I have suggested.
Consider the position of the mining industry. I do not believe the men in the mines have received a fair deal-far from it. I referred to this particular matter in 1923 and 1924 on my motion for a national coal supply. I believe in labour and have been a consistent supporter of labour since first entering the city council of Toronto. One of the things I value most highly is that, notwithstanding a life of much stress and strain in many
Post-War Reconstruction

spheres of activity, including municipal work, which is closer to the people than any other branch of government, I have always managed to retain the respect and support of the overwhelming majority of labour in the city I represent. With Sir Adam Beck, my former colleague, and Sir James Whitney, I went all over Ontario preaching the gospel of cheap light and power for the urban, suburban and rural workers. In the days before and during the great war we were attacked by some of our own newspapers in Ontario and called amateur anarchists, because we tried to restore the people of the province their heritage of cheap power and light, a policy which you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, supported in the great district of new Ontario. I believe that before the war is over, notwithstanding much of this talk about planning, the larger part of the work will devolve upon the municipalities.
Recently there was a long debate in the British House of Commons on this general subject, when empire trade, international affairs and other great issues were discussed. Here is what Admiral Southby said about post-war planning. He is a sincere friend of labour; he is a man of vision; he has predicted almost everything that has happened in the war:
It seems to me that the people who talk loudest about post-war equality are those who deny the right of anyone who disagrees with them to share in the planning of the new world, but I am certain of one thing, and it gives me great hope and courage. If the little man, who is the embodiment of British common sense and sanity, is capable, as he is, of destroying Hitler and Mussolini and all their works, he is quite capable, when the war is over, of destroying bureaucracy. He says in effect, in the words of Geoffrey Dobb:
We who in the ashes d-well Want no planned and ordered hell;
Fight no war to be policed
When the bombs and fires have ceased.
Life's too precious far to give For any freedom but to live.
That is exactly what the soldiers will want when they come home. The "little man", immortalized by Strube, who saved England, will know, when the war is over, how to plan for the future of the empire and of world trade, in the same way as he did to beat Hitler and Mussolini in the war.
I have almost finished. I will merely add that there was planning as long ago as the aftermath of the Napoleonic war. We all know the condition of the working classes after that great war, that women and children were working in the mines of the mother country in a living tomb below ground. Read the "History of England" by T. H. Green; 
note the condition of the mass of the working people after the war with Napoleon. The state of the workers at that time was disgraceful. Then came the industrial revolution, the union of coal and steel. What did it do? As Lord Perry has said:
The industrial revolution made it possible for any man to work his own way from poverty and illiteracy to a commanding position in both industry and the state. Richard Cobden is an outstanding example-the son of a Sussex farm labourer who became a great Lancashire manufacturer and a great statesman. William Cobbett is another example. In fact, industry and commerce during the nineteenth century produced such men not by the hundreds but by the thousands-careful, frugal men, hard of head and often hard of heart, but notable for two qualities above all others, diligence and selfreliance.
These men were self-trained into habits of clear commercial thinking, quick and bold decisions, personal responsibility and individual initiative. It -was no easy school. Those who lacked the necessary application or the necessary drive had short shrift. The age was kindly only to those who satisfied its needs.
I believe that the first thing to do after the war is to encourage private initiative and free enterprise. True it is that this will have to be brought up to date. I believe that when the soldiers come home they will want the rights that men enjoyed in the days of Macdonald and Laurier, when everybody owned some property-it might be a cow; it might be a small mill, or a country store, or a horse and wagon, but property of some kind. We have been slow to see that, with the right of acquiring private property denied to them, the people of Canada became proletarian. Their liberty passed away; it will have to be restored.
I believe in private initiative. I believe that the right to possess private property is derived from nature and not from man and that the state has no business to abolish it but only to regulate its use. And that, I believe, will be the view of our soldiers when they return.
At present the war is not won, and the war is the main issue to-day; all these other problems are secondary and will have to wait until the victory is ours. I do not object to planning; you can do all you like of it as long as it is not done at the exepnse of the war effort. But I plead with the government and with the committee not to forget that victory is our main purpose, and that without victory all the planning will amount to very little.
I thank the house for having listened so attentively. I have had some experience in matters of reconstruction and planning; it is not confined to my friends on the left, who

Post-War Reconstruction
of course are entitled to their views. And from practical experience I tell them that we shall have to go back, as they are doing in England, to supporting by legislation the retail man and the wholesaler. This was done in some degree in the pre-war trade practices act passed there to restore private enterprise. Give these people a chance to do their own business, wholesale and retail, in a businesslike way, and remove the barriers which have been erected in restraint of trade and have made it impossible for them to carry on in the past number of years.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I do not intend to inflict another speech on the house, but as a member of the committee last year I have a few remarks to make with respect to the machinery which is being put op for the purpose of working out our reconstruction plans. The reason why I am not going to impose anotl er speech on the house is that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) made quite a lengthy statement this afternoon and set out fairly clearly the views of this group on reconstruction plans in general, and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has just now given us an enlightening discourse on the matter, so that it will not be necessary for me to go into those details.
What I am interested in bringing to the attention of the minister who has been directing the work of this committee is the machinery which is being set up. My conception of the work done last year by the parliamentary committee is that it did all it could with the machinery provided for it, but that it merely scratched the surface and received some reports.
My objection to the whole set-up, and I think I voiced it to some extent last year both in the committee and in the house, is that I see the questions of reconstruction and rehabilitation as one problem, and I believe there are too many committees handling the research and other details without any clear understanding as to which committee will put these plans into final form, bring them back to this house and accept responsibility for them. The committee being set up under this resolution is the responsible committee to which the general public is looking for some comprehensive plans in connection with reconstruction and rehabilitation; and if we are to have any success the numerous committees dealing with the matter will have to have their authority and powers well defined.
For example, last session the canteen committee handled a phase of rehabilitation as applied to the soldier, and in my opinion a
very important phase, but I did not consider it a function of that committee, regardless of the fact that most of the committee members were ex-service men. We are now running into difficulties in connection with the legislation based upon the work of that committee, which was designed to protect the boy who left his job and went into the army by forcing the employer to see to it that the boy on his return was given the employment which he left when he enlisted. I have recently received numerous complaints from men who never had jobs, who are coming back to sections where trade unions that have seniority clauses written into their agreements are functioning. A boy in such a position cannot get a job without great difficulty. If he does succeed in getting one and a lay-off comes along-for there are lay-offs now-because he has no seniority in the plant he loses the job. Therefore we have really not provided, as far as that legislation is concerned, any security for the boys who come back.
Then there was the James committee, which sat for some. fifteen months and which was divided into subcommittees. The chairman of that committee came before the reconstruction committee and presented a fine report, but in my view it was mostly words, with no concrete suggestions as to what should be done in the field of reconstruction. That committee did some very good research work, but it merely brought back a report to the parliamentary committee. Some of the subcommittees of the James committee did not function at all, or at least did not report to the parliamentary committee. For instance, the committee on education and employment, one of the most important subcommittees, which was headed by Mr. Tom Moore, did not make a report. The explanation was that Mr. Moore was ill. That was quite true, but someone should have been appointed to take his place.
