speechtext: That has been done; Mr. Bengough has been appointed.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
That is good. We now find an economic advisory committee being set up, which in my opinion will practically usurp the powers of the James committee. The advisory committee is composed largely of deputy ministers; it is nothing more or less than an interdepartmental committee of the government doing research which in my opinion should be done by independent people reporting directly to the parliamentary committee to enable it to form and bring back to the house an independent report. I understand that in the Department of Pensions and National
Post-War Reconstruction

Health there is a departmental committee carrying on research and bringing in certain legislation by order in council with respect to soldiers returning from overseas. Therefore, when the minister makes his statement I think he should clearly state which committee is senior, and which committee will bring a report into the house. Will that committee be privileged to take advantage of all the research being done by the other committees and put it into a final report which will be brought to this house? If the parliamentary committee is to function in that way, then in my opinion it will have to be provided with a secretariat and the necessary machinery to carry on that work. That should be their function, since they are the elected members of the house and the public will look upon them as the responsible committee.
I should like to make just a few observations as to what I think are the basic problems with which we should start now and about which we should do something. Speechmaking will not solve the problem. As a member of the committee last year I think one of the first problems we shall have to tackle is that of the soldier returning from overseas. If the war should end to-morrow I would not want to see our army demobilized with the machinery we have at present for looking after them. When I think of that army overseas I try to place myself in the position of one of the soldiers for a few moments. Large numbers of the boys now in England never had jobs. They have been in the army now for three years, but to date no one in this country has told them that they will have jobs on. their return. We know that the Canadian army will be the spearhead when the time comes to cross the channel, and I do not think any of our men have any illusions as to what that job will rhean. Consequently it is only natural for a boy in that position to stop and think what he is facing certain death for. If we want to build up the morale of that army and of the Canadian people, we must do two things. We must guarantee those boys that if the war should terminate suddenly and they should return to Canada, they will not have to wrestle in the ranks of the unemployed or eke out an existence on $9 a week, as is provided by the regulations at present. They should . be told that the Canadian people are prepared to keep them in uniform on full pay and allowances, to give them vocational training and to route them into some gainful employment with a decent standard of living before they are finally taken off the Canadian payroll. That would guarantee to those boys
[Mr. Gillis.3
that when they came back, whether to-morrow or next year, the Canadian people would be prepared to recognize their responsibility at least to the extent of making sure that they would not have to go into the lines of the unemployed or those on relief. I am sure that would be good for the morale of our boys overseas.
In addition, I think this government should enact the New Zealand old age pension plan. I do not need to elaborate on that, for I am sure the minister is even more familiar with it than I am. Many of our boys overseas have fathers and mothers at home who are too young to qualify under the present regulations for the old age pension, but who are too old to work, who have broken down after years of heavy work and the worry of the last ten years of depression.
The only income in most of those homes is an assignment of pay and allowances granted by the government. Such a boy is in the position that if he goes under, fighting for democracy and freedom, he not only loses his life but throws his father and mother back on the relief rolls. That is no exaggeration; it is an actual fact; I have handled cases of that kind. A large percentage of our people are in that position. And that gesture of keeping him on the payroll, the enactment immediately of an old age pension that guarantees his father and mother means of existence, builds his morale to the point that at least the- war has brought about something, a guarantee that there will be no more relief roll for his father and mother and a recognition by us that he is entitled to something when he comes back and is not taking a chance of going on relief. Those two things should be done by the reconstruction committee as one of its first responsibilities.
Another matter we should immediately consider and make a pronouncement upon is this. There are thousands and thousands of employees in war industries, crown organizations carrying on war work only. If the war were suddenly to terminate, thousands of these people would face the street, and they realize it. If you go around among them you will find that that is what they are discussing. What are we going to do with respect to these crown emanations, these war industry plants, when the war is over? What plans are we making to convert them to peace-time pursuits?
These are three matters about which we should immediately do- something. It would tend to build up the morale of the soldiers overseas and of the Canadian people. These are basic problems of urgent importance and

Post-War Reconstruction
matters upon which the committee should make a pronouncement at once. There is no research necessary into these matters, except as to the conversion of war industries. The government is in a position with respect to most of these industries to say something about them; the other questions are merely matters of common, sense and something should be done about them immediately.
One thing we must realize is that we are not in a position similar to that of the last war. We are dealing to-day with a generation that has already gone through a war; that has seen the aftermath of war and that is not going through the same thing again. If our hon. friends on this side and those on the government side are not prepared to bring about changes in a sensible and logical way through the medium of the constitution that we have to-day, those changes will be brought about in some other way, a way we do not like. Let us not make any mistake about that or try to fool ourselves, because we shall be only fooling ourselves if we think in those terms.
I do not want to make a long speech. I wish to leave just those three points with the committee and to ask the minister for a clarification of the machinery we are providing in the field of reconstruction. In my own province thousands of men have left the basic industry there, coal mining. There has been quite a shrinkage in that industry since the outbreak of the war. I have some figures; I shall not bother the house with them now, but will bring them before the reconstruction committee. I know that if the men who have enlisted from that industry came back to-morrow or next. year there is no employment for them as far as I can see. Hundreds of boys left that section of the country who never had a job, and there is now no job for them there. There is only one way to ease the minds of these people. They know it; I receive many letters from overseas; they write to me on that point; they have no illusions about it. Without a pronouncement now that we are making provision for them against their return, until we can reorganize society and turn it back to peace-time pursuits, I would be afraid to see them come back. The reconstruction committee will go into that situation as far as that industry is concerned. The chairman was good enough to allow us to bring that whole situation to the attention of the committee last session. When we get under way again the operators should be summoned to meet that committee, to put their plans on the table face up and to let us know what the future holds with respect
to that industry and potential employment for men returning from overseas.
I merely wanted to bring these matters to the attention of the minister so that he might say something about them when he closes the debate.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
First
I wish to say a word as to the high note that has been sounded to-day in the debate that has so far taken place on the motion of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) that this reconstruction and reestablishment committee should be set up. I am not a bit surprised at the high tone of the speeches that have been made, not only because I know the great interest that is in the minds of all hon. members in the subject under discussion, but because, looking back to the conduct of that committee during last session, I am filled with a deep sense of appreciation of the friendliness and courtesy extended to me, who happened to be chairman of that committee, by all its members. We see to-night what the minister has recognized, because he attended faithfully the meetings of that committee during last session, namely, that every member of it is in dead earnest in the work which he has undertaken as a representative of the people.
Several points have been brought out so far in the debate. There is the question of what is generally called full-time employment and there is the question of full production. May I put on Hansard, for although it is on the record of the committee it has not yet been put upon Hansard, a resolution that was moved in that committee on June 30 last and was accepted by the committee. I happened to be the mover. That motion reads:
Whereas the most immediate reconstruction problem confronting Canada to-day is the creation of employment for and the settlement of returned soldiers and workers from war industry, and,
Whereas the proper development of our natural resources can provide both employment and settlement opportunities through irrigation, flood control, reforestation, the development of water power for industrial and other uses, the exploration of mineral and oil deposits, and the provision of transportation where-required by settlers or by industry:
Therefore be it resolved that this committee on reconstruction and reestablishment study the best means to bring about the proper utilization of the natural resources of Canada in such manner as will make it possible for the government of Canada, in cooperation with provinces and municipalities, to avail itself of every opportunity to create employment for, anil arrange the permanent and satisfactory settlement of, men and women discharged from our armed forces and from the merchant navy, and workers released from industry.

Post-War Reconstruction
I read that motion not only for the purpose of putting it upon the record of this house, but also because I think it is the foundation for a good deal of the work that must be done by the committee which is being set up. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to the fact that following that motion we went into a study of the development of the coal resources in Nova Scotia, and he hopes, as I hope, that when the committee is again at work that particular study will be continued. I believe that if we as a committee study the existing operation and utilization of our natural resources we shall be in a better position to judge the nature of the utilization and development of our natural resources that we as a committee on reconstruction should recommend to this house and through the house to the people of Canada.
I wish also to call attention to the fact that this resolution points out that we do these things, or some of them, in cooperation with the provinces and the municipalities. In a country with so complex a constitution as that of Canada, in a country whose national entity was, after all, created by resolutions of the provinces themselves, it is. absolutely essential that we should convey to the people our desire to work in conjunction with the provinces.
As a matter of fact, following that particular resolution, much work of a highly preparatory nature has been done by some of the provinces. During last session, as chairman of the committee I received many commendations from people in several provinces on the fact that our committee wanted to cooperate with them. If I may be permitted to speak for a moment about my own province of British Columbia I would call attention to the fact that the legislature of that province at its last session set up a post-war rehabilitation council consisting of members of all political parties. And apparently without thought of party advantage, that committee has carried on a positive work of preparation for the days of reconstruction. They have prepared a voluminous report, one which it seems to me is absolutely constructive. I am very happy to-night to pay one word of tribute, because the chairman of that committee, the Hon. Mr. Perry, provincial minister of education, is one of my constituents. The constituency of Fort George which he represents in the legislature is the centre of the federal constituency of Cariboo which I represent in this house. This booklet which I have in my hand happens to be the report, and I can say it is full of good meat, having to do with reconstruction.

Naturally, when one speaks of reconstruction there come to his mind two sets of thoughts, one relating to world structure and international undertakings, and the other to the new structure affecting the people of Canada themselves. It is not my intention to-night to say anything about world-wide structure, except to throw out this thought, that I agree-and I speak as a member of the House of Commons and a member of the reconstruction committee-with the suggestion of Vice-President Wallace of the United States, that when war is over we must have a system of collective security which will guarantee to the people of every nation the same application of the rule of law in international affairs as we now enjoy within our own country in domestic affairs.
Our own continued process of armament and preparation for war and the process followed by each individual nation will to a large extent depend upon the nature and the condition of that collective security which can be given to every people by the combination of nations. So far as the preparation for reconstruction is concerned, I agree and always have agreed with what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, namely, that the first great task confronting us as the House of Commons and as a people is the conduct of the war itself. It is not necessary for me to say to any hon. member that it is useless for us to prepare for reconstruction, if in doing so we do not continue to make certain that by every possible means we conduct our war effort properly; because if we lose the war the reconstruction period will be developed not by us but by those nations which defeat us in the war. And if we are not successful; if we do not win the war by a proper invasion of axis countries, by the annihilation of their military strength and by the total subjugation of their military caste, but have to arrange a peace through negotiation, then the terms of reconstruction will not be made by us, because conditions will obtain over which we shall not be masters.
The only real reason, then, for thinking of reconstruction is to think of it in such terms whereby what we are doing and what we are saying will of themselves aid in the prosecution of the war.
I take kindly to the suggestion made tonight, namely, that we as a parliamentary committee should take steps to let our boys and women know overseas what we are trying to do.
Mention was made of what will happen when the offensive takes place, an offensive of which, as has been said before, the Canadian soldier

Post-War Reconstruction
will be the spearhead. We cannot blind ourselves to the fact that while the men and women who are there are anxious to play their full part for Canada, they know that a good many of them will not return to their families. It is our duty to let them know that we, the members of the House of Commons, intend by every possible means to see that what takes place after this war will not be in line with what was permitted to take place during the last one.
Here I wish to say a word of commendation respecting the Minister of Pensions and National Health. We can look back over the last two or three years and see things done for enlisted men, men who offered to give everything they have, including their lives. We can see a vast difference in the life being planned for them and that which was permitted to apply to the soldiers and their dependents who survived the last war. I say that in commendation of the present minister.
I leave that phase of the matter with the thought that between the two great wars, in what we were pleased to call the days of peace -and I say this without criticism of any political party or any minister-in those days of fabricated peace we as public men, and those who were then public men, thought more of money and taxation than we did of human values. A government was judged successful, not by the things it did or arranged to do for human welfare, but by the small amount of money it expended, and the manner in which it kept the rate of taxation down. That was the judgment not only of men in public life, but of most people in Canada. We the people of Canada failed in that, just as we failed to prepare for a war that some of us-all of us- should have seen was coming upon us.
Having said that, I wish to say a few words about the northwestern section of Canada. I know I shall be forgiven if it happens that the part of the country to which I intend to refer comes within the constituency of Cariboo. I make this reference not only because my very good friend the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) spoke so eloquently respecting that country and urged the minister to make certain preparations for the future by the development of the natural resources within that great terrain, but because I want to speak of more than the development of natural resources and what they might mean in employment and production. We have to-day the greatest cooperation between two nations that perhaps the history of the world has ever seen. I am speaking of that which exists between Canada and the United States. When Mr. Roosevelt, President of the United States, and the Prime
Minister of Canada met at Ogdensburg in August, 1940, to arrange for the setting up of a joint defence commission, many people thought that would apply only to the defence of North America. But it has developed pace by pace until to-day we see the realization of what has been described lately in this city as the realization of the age-long dream of the northwest passage.
Mention has been made to-night of the air lanes. How many people in Canada realize that the new air lanes now in operation across Canada and fed from the United States which head directly toward Japan-if I may digress for a moment may I say that I hope they will prove to be a channel of offensive action against Japan-mean that the distance from Chicago or Montreal to Tokyo and Shanghai is over 2,000 miles less than the old route through San Francisco which was in operation up to the time of this war. Any distance of over 2,000 miles means a great deal even when one is thinking of aeroplanes and the great speed which they have reached.
There have been expenditures of huge sums of United States money in the Yukon and British Columbia. We have United States soldiers in the Yukon and British Columbia, and there are Canadian soldiers in Alaska. They are all operating together. A joint commission has been appointed to study the proper means of dealing with the facilities which have been created for war purposes in British Columbia, the Yukon and Alaska and the proper joint utilization and development of the natural resources of those lands. I wish I could presume upon the patience of the house to deal at greater length with some of the matters mentioned to-night by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). I am tempted to do so because what he said relates so keenly to my own constituency, to that of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) and to that of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Sissons). I cannot take the time of the house for this. I want, however, to leave in your mind, Mr. Speaker, the thought that not only have we opened up a northwest passage to Japan, China and the other oriental countries, but we have created a great international cooperative movement between Canada and our great neighbour, the United States.
As was pointed out to-night, in addition to thinking in terms of general reconstruction problems we must also be concrete. The resolution adopted by the committee last session is in itself a concrete foundation upon which a great structure can be built. There is oh the order paper a resolution standing
Post-War Reconstruction

in the name of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) which asks this house to pass legislation enlarging the scope of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Members of the committee will remember that during the hearings last session I asked the committee to sit in camera because I did not want too much press publicity. I then suggested that the committee should study the advisability of recommending to the house that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act should be extended in its general scope and operation. It deals now only with the three prairie provinces, and in my opinion the committee should recommend that it deal with all Canada and that its general scope be enlarged. The hon. member for Medicine Hat is a member of the committee, and I suggest that he lay this matter before the committee when it meets again. Some means must be suggested by which there can be a proper utilization and development of our natural resources. I believe the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has been fairly successful on the prairies and I believe its extension to cover all Canada would also be successful.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) referred to the numerous committees on reconstruction which have been in operation, I agree with him that the committee of the house, which is built upon the representation of the people of Canada themselves, is the main committee. But I agree also with the minister that it has been essential for other committees to be at work. The committee which has been described to-night and which has been working under the auspices of the Minister of Pensions and National Health had a secretariat, research advisers and research counsel. These men have been working all the time; they have been able to make studies and possibly are in a position to recommend conclusions to a greater extent than could the House of Commons committee.
We secured from that committee and from the minister some excellent statements covering not only the things that have been done by the government but the matters under study by the committee and by departmental officers. I feel certain that when our committee is ready to start its work again the minister will see to it that we have the benefit of all the studies whch have been made by his departmental officials and by members of that committee. I do not know if I am permitted to say this or not, but I understand that the other house is also setting up a committee on reconstruction. As a member

of our committee I welcome that, and I feel sure that we shall be able to cooperate with each other.
Mention was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) to the statement made to the American Federation of Labor convention by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I want to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for the nature of the address he gave to this, house. He quoted the Prime Minister as follows:
I believe the war is teaching us that the obstacles to full employment were not real obstacles; that a partnership of management, of workers and of the community can make useful work available, in time of peace no less than in time of war, for all who need or want to work.
I am afraid the hon. member took a wrong meaning from the Prime Minister's statement. As I interpret his speech, he meant what everybody in this house thinks he meant. There is not any question that during the terrible and long years after the war which were known as the depression we let ourselves sink to depths of shame which only the courage, heroism and sacrifices of the men and women who are fighting for us overseas can wipe out. What the Prime Minister was saying to himself as well as to the men and women whom he was actually addressing was that the experiences of the war-and surely we must learn from the experiences of the war-have taught us that we, business men as well as the government, permitted certain things to be obstacles to full employment in the days of peace, when, had we only known it, those things were not real obstacles.
Something was said to-night about the necessity for a declaration. The declaration is there. The obstacle is declared to be an imaginary obstacle, and we realize it now. If there is any man in this house to-day who thinks we can ever have a similar depression in Canada, let me say to him that we have all across Canada a farming population which from its pioneering days has been imbued with courage and with experience. During the last three years of war our industrialists, management and labour, have shown what they can do when there is a real objective before them, and we have a realization to-day that never again will it be necessary for the people of Canada to be in want.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: It never was necessary.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I am not saying that it
was. I am saying that what we allowed to be obstacles were false obstacles.

Post-War Reconstruction
Let me say to some who I am afraid are thinking not of the material problems as much as of great principles, and I say this so that every member of the house will know where I stand, that I for my part am a believer in free enterprise. You may call it capitalism, if you like; I am a believer in it. I say as a member of this house and as a member of the committee, but I say this to the industrialists and to the business men and to every man and woman in Canada who are believers in free enterprise, that in my interpretation of systems as well as of terms, free enterprise does not pertain only to those who are in big business. The right of free enterprise pertains to every man and to every woman, to the farmer and to the labourer, to the small business man as well as to the big business man.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext: Let them exercise it.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
All right. We are talking now of the reconstruction committee, and I say that I approve more than I can say the announcement in the speech from the throne of the setting up of another committee to deal with social security. That is necessary. I agree with many of the provisions of the Beveridge report, but again speaking as a member of parliament I say that that is not enough. I have just pointed out that I am a believer in free enterprise, but I say that in addition to social security measures we must have fundamental changes. Those fundamental changes must be of such a nature as to give to government at least a motivating influence, if not a directive influence. We must have fundamental changes which will permit the farmer and the labouring man to have the benefit of free enterprise, and which will make a connecting link between agriculture and industry, between industry and government, and between government and agriculture. When I speak of industry I do not mean only capital and management; I mean industry as composed of capital and management and labour. I for my part am ready to state that in my opinion it is against sound public policy to permit plants employing large numbers of men to operate without provision for collective bargaining by the employees. That is, I think labour in its organized form must be a substantive part of the industry itself, and from the days of the end of the war onwards, when we speak of industry, we must mean labour in its organized form as well as industry itself. I hope we can have a condition here in Canada where social security as it relates to the men and women who are employed in industry will be taken care of by industry itself, but I do not think we can secure that at the moment. I consider, however, that that is the proper place to begin with social and economic security for the men and women who are employed in industry. But we cannot reach that condition unless we-and by "we" I mean parliament and government, provincial as well as dominion -recognize that organized labour is an actual part of industry itself. We must realize and recognize that the foundation of our whole economy rests with the farmers of the land, because industry, even considered as management and labour, cannot operate properly unless agriculture is on a sound basis. It therefore becomes, in my opinion, the duty of the reconstruction committee to take every possible step, in addition to what I have said about industry and labour, to put farming on a proper basis. If we do that, and if we bring about the developments of which the hon. member for Davenport has spoken so eloquently to-night, we can look forward to the post-war period without fear if, in addition, we let our fighting men who are overseas know what we are trying to do.
I have spoken of the unbearable conditions under which the men who fought in the last war and their dependents were living before this war commenced. We forgot the human values. We realized that as a result of that war Canada had taken a higher place than before in the galaxy of the nations of the world. But we forgot that our place in the world rested upon a foundation of broken hearts, shattered men, and our immortal dead. When this war is over I hope we shall realize that the glory that then will be ours in still greater measure will rest upon the same three things-the broken hearts of the women and children left behind, the shattered lives of the men who come back from the brink of the grave, and the immortal dead in such large numbers who will never see their homes again.
I say, in conclusion, that when this war is over and our men return to us from the graves of Europe or of Asia or of other lands where many of their comrades will lie forever, I hope that with the aid of the returned soldier organizations, the churches of the land, ministers of governments and members of parliament we shall never again be permitted to forget that our national glory will rest upon the sacrifices that have been made by our soldiers.
I want to express through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, and through him to the government my appreciation as a public man of what has been done in the last two years and of what is to be done in the future, and to express the hope that, when the war is over and we have
Post-War Reconstruction

won it properly, our post-war problems will not actually prove to be as acute as now we think they may be.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
It gives me very great pleasure to speak on this resolution to set up this committee which obviously has such general support from all parts of the house.
There is just one suggestion I should like to make to the minister before I proceed, namely, that a considerable amount of work on reconstruction has already been done, and a certain amount of the job necessary to do is now known. I suggest to the minister that before the committee brings down its report he should act on the suggestions which have already been put before him by the James committee and the other committee on reconstruction. In this connection I particularly want to recommend to his attention the findings of the Guelph conference on soil erosion in old Ontario.
Nobody appreciates more than I do the necessity of having blueprints ready before the need to build is apparent. At the Guelph conference the situation existing in Ontario was carefully gone into, but it was brought out by all the experts who spoke and presented papers that very little actual survey work had been done. Only King township and the Ganaraska valley had been at all adequately surveyed; that is, not more than two hundred square miles out of seventy-five thousand which needed to be surveyed. The rest of that territory must be surveyed before any comprehensive plan of soil conservation and reforestation can be undertaken. That is not a job which can be done in a minute; it is a job for expert scientists, for men who are trained to do that work. I realize that at the moment such men are extremely difficult to get, and I would suggest to the minister that as many as possible of these survey parties be sent into the rest of that part of Ontario during the coming summer, not waiting until after the report has been brought down. It is estimated by the Guelph conference, and particularly by Professor Coventry, who was one of the speakers at the conference, that it would require about two hundred survey parties adequately to cover those seventy-five thousand square miles of Ontario and that the survey alone would occupy three years. The necessity of that work is well known. We must do something about it; otherwise that part of Ontario will become a desert. I would suggest with the utmost emphasis that these survey parties be started and put at work this summer season.
There is one other matter as to which, I think, immediate work could be undertaken.

Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that this is in any way the total or even a major part of the work of the committee. I consider this committee to be one of the most if not the most important of the committees set up in this house. But there is work which we know already has to be done. In the metropolitan district of Toronto, which includes all of York county and probably the. adjoining counties, the architectural association has estimated that to provide a comprehensive plan of re-housing that area will take as long as two years, and it will cost in the neighbourhood of $100,000. I mention these figures merely to emphasize the size of the job which lies ahead of us.
These are things which I suggest we should be doing. A start-making the blueprints, providing the plans-should be made at once. We cannot risk being unprepared at the end of the war. We cannot take the chance of our army coming back from Europe and our war industries suddenly shutting off and leaving our men in the street. We must have those plans, and in my opinion there is not a moment to lose. I agree with everything that has been said in this chamber concerning the seriousness of the war situation. I realize- nobody, probably, better-what a tough job lies ahead of us to win the war. But because I do that, I also realize what a difficult, long and complicated job the reconstruction committee has in front of it, and it is because I do not wish to see any time wasted that I make these suggestions to the minister.
In the coming years of reconstruction in Canada, I believe we shall discover that the findings in England of the Uthwatt report will affect us far more than the Beveridge report. The way in which in England they have conserved their land, and now-this is the finding of Mr. Justice Uthwatt-are growing between two-thirds and three-quarters of the food necessary for that island, whereas at one time they grew only one-third of their requirements, is an indication of how far we can go in the matter of land through proper land use. Nobody has been more prodigal of the land than we in Canada. One would think in some places we had deliberately set out to destroy the farms and the land. In some places in King township they found that the land had been lumbered, the timber taken off it; that it had been farmed and it had become waste land, within one generation. The first settler within one generation cut the trees, farmed the land, and was so careless of the land that it is now abandoned.
This is one of the most serious things facing Canada to-day. I shall not go into details,

Post-War Reconstruction
but I will say this, that unless we take immediate steps to see to it that forest cover is put back on the land, that erosion is stopped, that streams like the Etobicoke, the Ganaraska and the Grand river do not lose sixty or seventy per cent of their water in a spring freshet of two or three days, we are in very grave danger of having our land turn into a desert. It is because this has been so deeply impressed upon me that I make the plea that the minister waste no time in setting up these extra surveys in order to tackle this one specific job.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the discussion on this subject, and I am wondering whether most of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken have not missed the real implications of the resolution now before the house. Much and, in fact, all that has been said has been sound and helpful, but we are not here dealing with a resolution having in view the reconstruction of a county or even a nation. At the conclusion of hostilities we shall face a world that will have been seriously bruised, and the fact is that interdependence will stare us in the face even more intensely after the conflict is over than at any time during the last three decades.
The approach to this problem of reconstruction must be, not in terms of adequate measures of public works, and that sort of thing, but in terms of the kind of world, let alone the kind of country, in which we shall live. That, I think, is the basic consideration in this discussion.
Let me say at the outset that I share the view expressed by those who have thus far spoken, that one need make no apology for this resolution or this debate. It is true that in some quarters it is suggested that this is no time to deal with the post-war period, that all our energies should be concentrated on the one problem of winning the war. With that, of course, we shall all agree; but winning the war will require the use of various instruments. No one now in the light of history will say that when Wilson introduced his fourteen points the programme which he offered did not have a definite relation to the victory which ultimately came about. It was a means of encouraging nations that were seriously disturbed as to whether they should give their support. To-day, if we have an adequate programme, as Mr. Morrison said yesterday when speaking in the United Kingdom, because of that very programme we may save much bloodshed and perhaps shorten the war. For there are many people in various parts of the world, in' Europe and particularly in Asia, who are not
convinced that the united nations offer the best solution in the post-war period. The man who was born and brought up in the east has learned in many respects to suspect the white man and his rule, and there are nations in Europe that feel, perhaps less tensely but none the less surely, a somewhat similar motivation. Therefore, in the prosecution of this war it is up to us at the same time to arrive at some approaches-perhaps they can be no more than approaches-which will convince the conquered nations of Europe and those of the east now dominated by the enemy that because of our history and civilization and because of our programme, we may offer them much more in connection with their personal and national rehabilitation.
I noticed one vein running through the speeches of hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. The other day in the excellent speech of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) there was expressed the thought that we must clearly define our aims, that otherwise the energy which was being put into the fight might be unavailing. The hon. member seemed to suggest that there was a definite connection between the reasons which brought us into the fight and the sort of world Tvhich many of us would set up afterwards. I suggest that the hon. gentleman is wrong, that in his mind there was a confusion between the provocation of the war and our peace aims. There can be no doubt as to why we engaged in this tremendous struggle. We did so simply because there were in existence certain forces that were prepared to bring to an end our type of civilization; men who were ready to stop at nothing to achieve great power and great expansion in empire at the expense of decency and civilization itself. That is the reason and the only reason why we engaged in this conflict; and to suggest that we did so in order to build a better world is unintentionally to give Hitler an assumption which he does not deserve. Surely we would have gone on with these plans of reform whether or not the war had come. It may be that the war has brought about a more ready realization of their implications, but surely these plans would have been contemplated by people throughout the world whether or not Hitler had risen to power. Therefore we are fighting, not to build a better world, but to rid the world of a force, a cancer, which prevents the realization of these better things.

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
Would not both our allies and the conquered peoples be greatly encouraged if they knew that when we had rid the world of this force we were going to bring about something better?
Post-War Reconstruction

maintopic: POST-WAR RECONSTRUCTION APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON RECONSTRUCTION AND REESTABLISHMENT
speechtext:
I quite agree, and that is our justification for considering these problems at this time. The committee on reconstruction of which I have the privilege of being a member has a great job to do, and I must say that several of the suggestions advanced by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) meet -with my approval. In the first place it seems to me that a committee so important requires assistance which the membership of this house alone cannot give. We have the James committee and other non-parliamentary committees composed of various deputy ministers and the like; we have the group in the Department of External Affairs, who are cooperating with many other official agencies of the United Nations. It seems to me the work of the committee would be greatly assisted by the setting up of some efficient, though not necessarily a large personnel research committee or secretariat which could follow up many of the threads which the members of the committees are not equipped or have not time to deal with. There is, however, one thing I believe the committee must not overlook, and it is this. The broad aspect of this problem will not be solved merely by considering palliatives of the sort we had to consider under the shadows of the New Deal both in this country and in other countries, particularly the United States.
The problem is much deeper and broader than that. There is the whole political aspect of the problem Here we have a United Nations scheme, a machinery of action by which on the political side we are trying to offset the strategy, political and military, of the enemy. I am not satisfied that the United Nations scheme for the purpose of carrying on the war is as strong as I should like. I should prefer to see greater emphasis on the United Nations aspect during the conflict than we now have. I could not help agreeing with many of the things which the hon. 'member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), speaking in the debate the other day, said when he referred to Casablanca with its advantages, yet with its apparent disadvantages. There was not full expression there of the voice of the United Nations. But if, when the war is over, the machinery of the United Nations is not functioning to the extent that we should like to see it function, think of the dangers we shall fall into at the conclusion, when there will be a tendency towards divergence on the part of the United Nations rather than of convergence. That is extremely important.
This committee therefore will have to consider the political implications of its work.

Mr. Morrison yesterday, quite properly I think, because he is a member of a government, one of the important governments in the United Nations group, nevertheless taking the cue from Mr. Welles and Mr. Hull, spoke of the kind of association that must prevail if at the conclusion of hostilities and during the period of liquidation and demobilization when we shall deal with refugee problems and the like, there is to be some order. Then, dealing with the long term, he spoke of the necessity of providing agencies by which the nations will act in concert and not on a competitive basis. Will our committee ignore this problem? Thus far in the deliberations of our committee we have dealt, quite properly but almost exclusively, with problems which in turn depend for their solution upon the settlement of the bigger problems. Must we not take into account that it comes within our ambit to consider whether the old agencies of collective security shall be maintained, or whether we are to build on the old foundation, whether we shall have regional organizations or whether these regional organizations will be simply economic structures? Those are considerations which I trust this committee will not hesitate to deal with fully.
The hon. member for Vancouver East to-day referred to that well-known book, "Conditions of Peace," by Edward Hallett Carr. That book has been widely circularized, more perhaps than many other books. I want to suggest this to the hon. member- perhaps in making this statement one will be accused of a certain amount of generality, but I make it nevertheless, for the same reason that Mr. Carr makes it; it is the underlying assumption of his book. The hon. member for Vancouver East to-day spoke about the necessity of bringing about economic and social reform. I do not quarrel with him on that. I do not wish to get into a discussion now as to whether I am in favour of a system of free enterprise or one of collectivism. I think in the future these labels will have little value, that we are likely to have a combination of both forms. But what I say and what Mr. Carr says is this:
The essential nature of the crisis through which we are now living is neither military, nor political, nor economic, but moral. A new faith in a new moral purpose is required to reanimate our political and economic system.
It is not simply a question of dollars and cents, it is not simply of economic security, although those things are important; it is a question of a rededication of what democ

racy really means, a rededication of the generally accepted religious conception and

War Appropriation
convictions of civilized1 men that must be at the base of the economic and social system which we are going to set up.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this. This problem of the kind of world we shall have may engage the philosopher. Our job is simply to realize that we have certain common objectives to attain. First, the immediate job will be to provide that the man who has borne the primary responsibility for carrying on the *war, the man who offered his life on the field of battle, shall be able when he returns to come back to a position where he will be able to compete at least equally with the civilian who was not called upon to bear that kind of sacrifice. I believe that the government, through the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), has a programme, not perfect, but a programme that should commend itself to this house generally, a programme based upon inquiry and an honest approach on the part of various committees of this house.
I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
